title: Railroad Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 3 3/4 × 2 9/16 × 1/16 in. (9.53 × 6.51 × 0.16 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this creatively shaped hotel room key token for room #33 during a stop along the Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railroad line at Van Horne, Iowa. The token has no date, Owney traveled through Iowa several times during his travels, and it could have been given to him anytime between 1888 and 1897.

title: St. Louis, Missouri Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/16 × 1 5/16 in. (3.33 × 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this Columbian half dollar coin from St. Louis, Missouri, postmaster J. B. Harlow on May 24, 1894. Columbian half dollars were popular collecting coins at the time. The first US commemorative issue coins, they were minted for the Chicago World’s Fair of 1893.

title: Charles W. Miller’s Coach and Baggage Express Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 × 1 5/8 in. (4.13 × 4.13 cm)
descriptions: There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney. The tag is from Charles W. Miller’s Coach and Baggage Express rail service, located in Buffalo, New York, in the late nineteenth century.

title: Corry, Pennsylvania Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: This coin given to Owney to wear as a tag is marked “25 cents, 1879” on one side, the numbers surrounded by a crown and leaf border. On the reverse are the names of the individuals who presented Owney with the coin; C. M. Hall and M. B. Bently of Corry, Pennsylvania. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Atlanta, Georgia Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney by the staff or proprietor of the Ballard Transfer company of Atlanta, Georgia. The tag was originally manufactured by W. W. Wilcox of Chicago, which was a major manufacturer of railroad baggage tags and similar metal items in the late nineteenth century. The Wilcox company manufactured other baggage tags that were presented to Owney.

title: E. Willmunder Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: This round metal tag marks Owney’s visit to Gallup, New Mexico. E. Willmunder presented the tag to Owney, as marked on the front and back sides of it. Mr. Willmunder was a member of the Knights of the Pythias, a fraternal organization devoted to benevolent activities that began in Washington, DC, in 1864 and continues in operation. The organization’s symbols include the knight’s head and cross guard finial. The initials F.C.B. stand for friendship, charity, and benevolence. Mr. Willmunder’s association with the Post Office Department or a railway line is currently unknown, nor is it known when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Camden and Amboy Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: There is no information on when this tag which was originally manufactured by W. W. Wilcox of Chicago in 1879 was given to Owney. It marks his travels on the Camden and Amboy Railroad in New Jersey. The Wilcox company was a major manufacturer of railroad baggage tags and similar metal items in the late nineteenth century. At least two other Owney tags were manufactured by the company.

title: Sweet's Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 × 1 5/8 in. (4.13 × 4.13 cm)
descriptions: There is no information on when Owney received this tag. It was given to him during a visit to Sweet’s Hotel in Grand Rapids, Michigan. The hotel was built by Martin Sweet in 1856.

title: Hotel Chilburg Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (4.45 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney by the staff or proprietor of the Hotel Chilburg. Owney received it on one of his visits to Tacoma, Washington. He visited Tacoma at least twice -- when he began and ended his 1895 trip around the world.

title: Corry, Pennsylvania Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 × 1 1/2 in. (4.45 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this brass tag while in Corry, Pennsylvania. The names of the individuals who presented him with the tag are indicated on the front and back. They are C.E. Bently, J.E. Gould, and S.W. Reese. Reese listed his company’s name, Reese and Co., as 182 Fulton Street, New York. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Seattle Central Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney. He received it from the staff or proprietor of the Seattle Central Hotel during a visit to Seattle, Washington.

title: San Francisco, California Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
descriptions: This token, marked good for 5-cent drink, was presented to Owney in San Francisco. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney. The token could have been redeemed at Fred Van Ordt’s saloon that was located at Jackson & Battery streets in San Francisco. The token is marked at the bottom by L.M. Moise, San Francisco.

title: Owney tag with entwined letters
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 x 1 3/4 in. (3.49 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: This series of entwined letters is unlike any of the other Owney tags. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, nor what the entwined letters represent.

title: San Francisco, California Owney Tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: The design of this oval-shaped metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. This tag is labeled Capt. W. Poole, San Francisco, California. The origin of this tag is unknown.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, nor who presented it to him and where. The tag’s markings are the letters R & U, the number 20, and the initials BH. BH could indicate the baggage handling portion of a train car.

title: A and CRAU marked Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: This small, brass tag is poorly marked with the letters "A" and "CRAU." There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, who presented it to the dog, or where.

title: Mankato, Minnesota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: J.C. Wise presented Owney with this round brass medal to wear as a tag while the dog was visiting Mankato, Minnesota. The date of the visit is indicated as June 17, 1895.

title: Express Saloon token, Cloverdale, California Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token, good for one drink or cigar from C. E. Mitchell’s “Express Saloon.” Mitchell emigrated from Germany in 1858, settling down in Cloverdale, California. His saloon may have been a popular stop for railway and railway mail workers working on board the San Francisco and Northern Pacific Railroad. This type of token is known as a trade check. These tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

title: Bank of St. Helena Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 x 1 5/8 in. (1.59 x 4.13 cm)
descriptions: This token was given to Owney in St. Helena, California during his travels on the Central Pacific Railroad. The token advertises a $1.00 reward for the return of the item it would have been attached to. Tokens such as these, commonly known as key tokens, were used to identify their owners in case of loss. There is no date to indicate when this was given to Owney. The key token’s text instructs that the item should be returned to the Bank of St. Helena in St. Helena, California.

title: Stude's Coffee Parlor Houston Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: This is one of two tokens Owney received from Alphonse Stude’s Houston, Texas, bakery. Stude, a prominent Houston businessman and city booster, recognized the advertising potential of the traveling dog. Usually Owney’s arrival to a town was heralded in the local newspaper and the articles about his welcome often listed the tokens he was wearing. This token, which could be used in trade for a cup of coffee, is known as a trade check. These tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

title: Indian Head Penny Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 × 3/4 in. (1.91 × 1.91 cm)
descriptions: This 1893 US coin, known as an “Indian head penny,” was one of several coins given to Owney during his travels. There is no record of when, or where, the dog received this token.

title: Travelers Preferred Accident Association Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while in Chicago, the most active railway town in the United States. The donor was from the “Travelers Preferred Accident Association,” a well known insurance company of the time. There is no additional information indicating the name of the donor or the date Owney received this token. This style of identification token was often attatched to items, such as keys, that might be lost.

title: Shea & Weaver Louisville, Kentucky Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token for 5-cents off of goods from the Shea & Weaver store in Louisville, Kentucky. There is no additional information to indicate when the token was given to the dog. Trade check tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

title: Saloon Token Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: There is no information to indicate the individual who gave Owney this token, “good for 5-cents at [the] bar.” The initials “L.J.S.” appear on the reverse side. This token, is known as a trade check. These tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

title: Seattle Transfer Company Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 2 1/8 x 1 13/16 x 1/16 in. (5.4 x 4.6 x 0.16 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check token from a railway station in Seattle, Washington. There is no additional information to indicate when the token was given to the dog. Owney visited Seattle on several occasions during his lifetime.

title: G&C railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: This small aluminum tag is marked G & C RR / New on the front side. There are no markings on the back side. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, who gave it to him, or where.

title: Brunswick Token Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token for 5-cents off from “The Brunswick,” an establishment located at “15 W. Gay” street in an unidentified city. There is no additional information to indicate when or where this token was added to Owney’s collection. This token, is known as a trade check. These tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

title: George Washington Medal Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 × 1/8 in. (3.8 × 3.8 × 0.3 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this advertising token from an unknown donor. The token celebrates President George Washington on one side, including an image and his birth and death dates, and aluminum, on the other. The U.S.’s first large aluminum refinery appeared in 1888, and the medal began to be used for tokens a few years later. The medal made its big splash with the American public at the Chicago World’s Fair in 1893. James Murdock, Jr. was already manufacturing tokens in brass, copper, and silver by the early 1890s and eagerly added aluminum to his business. This advertising token touts the metal on the back as “the new metal aluminum extracted from the common clay of the earth.” Murdock’s business was located in Cincinnati, Ohio.

title: Thomas Metcalf Saloon Token Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token for 5-cents off of goods from Thomas Metcalf, a merchant of unknown goods or services. There is no additional information to indicate when or where the token was given to the dog. This token, is known as a trade check. These tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

title: Leland House Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3 1/4 × 3 1/4 in. (8.26 × 8.26 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key token from the Leland House hotel in Winnipeg, Manitoba. The original number, 16, was scratched out and replaced with the number 51. The hotel was the city’s largest and most prominent hotel of the age. A few of Owney’s railway journeys took him into Canada, including one that took him aboard the Canadian Pacific railroad.

title: Nashville, Tennessee Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 2 3/16 × 1 3/4 × 1/16 in. (5.56 × 4.45 × 0.16 cm)
descriptions: Many of Owney’s travels were celebrated in local newspapers. Newspaper reporters were second only to postal employees in their interest in the wandering canine. Owney received this token from the Nashville Banner, a newspaper that was published in Nashville, Tennessee from 1876-1998. The token notes that it was presented to the dog in April 1892.

title: Canadian Pacific Railway Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 3/8 x 1 7/8 in. (6.03 x 4.76 cm)
descriptions: Owney occasionally traveled on Canadian railways, including the eastern portion of the Canadian Pacific Railroad. This baggage token, marked “Special P. 2847” was given to Owney during one of his trips on that railroad. The “Special” marking was used for travelers whose baggage would follow their journey off of the main railway onto another line. Railroad companies had agreements to return these specially marked tokens to the railroad of origin.

title: Hotel Occidental Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3 1/4 × 3 1/4 in. (8.26 × 8.26 cm)
descriptions: The locations of some of the tokens Owney received on his journeys are impossible to track down. This flowery metal token offers few clues to its origin. “Occidental” was a popular name for hotels in the late nineteenth century--no other information on this token provides a clue as to where Owney received this strikingly-shaped hotel key token.

title: Leland House Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5 x 2 3/4 in. (12.7 x 6.99 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token from a hotel called the “Leland House.” There were at least three hotels in the U.S. with that name during Owney’s lifetime, and nothing on the token indicates which city was home to this particular hotel.

title: Hotel Key Check Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 4 x 3 in. (10.16 x 7.62 cm)
descriptions: The locations of some of the tokens Owney received on his journeys are impossible to track down. This diamond-shaped metal token is marked simply “E 33 H” and offers no clues to its origin. It is similar in markings to hotel key tokens Owney received along his journeys, but without additional information it is impossible to definitively identify it as such.

title: Railway Mail Service Washington, D.C. Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 x 1 3/4 in. (5.4 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from James E. White’s office. White served as the General Superintendent of the Railway Mail Service from 1890 to 1907. The token, dated April 13, 1892, is a reminder of the admiration and respect Owney held in even the highest office of the nation’s Railway Mail Service.

title: B. & P.T. Co. Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 3/4 × 1 1/2 × 1/16 in. (4.4 × 3.81 × 0.16 cm)
descriptions: According to the information available on this token, Owney received it from a line or company known by the initials B&P, located in or near El Paso. The item, probably a baggage check token, does not provide enough information to indicate where or when it was given to the dog.

title: Manitoba Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token during one of his trips into Canada. The token was used in a grand hotel’s coat room. The Manitoba was a large seven-story, fashionably furnished hotel built in Winnipeg, the capital of Manitoba Province, Canada. The hotel, built about 1890 on Water Avenue, was destroyed less than a decade later in a fire in 1899. The hotel was a convenient stop for Owney, as it had been funded by the Northern Pacific and Manitoba Railway (N.P. & M.R.) and was located next to the N.P. & M.R. offices.

title: Lawrence, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 3 in. (5.72 x 7.62 cm)
descriptions: While visiting Lawrence, Massachusetts on June 13, 1894, Owney received a very personalized token. Those who gave the dog this token engraved a poem on it for all to see: “At Lawrence Mass. they took me in. And fed me well. It wasn’t thin. To the M. L. & B. north, they sent me then. And I hope to see them all again.” The MB&L was the Manchester, Lawrence & Boston Railway Post Office line.

title: New York Post Office Owney Tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 13/16 × 3 1/8 × 1/16 in. (4.6 × 7.94 × 0.16 cm)
descriptions: Owney may have received this token from a letter carrier. The token is actually a cap badge style worn by U.S. letter carriers of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The badge is number 73 from the Brooklyn, New York, post office. There is no additional information to indicate the name of the person who gave this token to Owney, or when it was received. The city of Brooklyn was one Owney visited several times during his travels, and he received at least seven tokens during those visits.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: There is not enough information on this token to indicate when or where it was given to Owney. It may be an Egyptian coin, and if so, would have been given to the dog during his around the world adventure in the fall of 1895.

title: Hotel Snoqualmie Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney may have received this token for room #137 of the Hotel Snoqualmie while visiting Seattle, Washington. A hotel of that name was located on Pike Street near 1st Avenue in Seattle in the early to mid 1890s. During his lifetime, Owney made a number of trips to the cities of Seattle and Tacoma, Washington, including his famous 1895 August trip, when he set out from Tacoma to travel with mailbags around the world.

title: Chinook, Montana Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token on May 14, 1893. The donor inscribed his initials on the back side of the token, “B.E.N.” along with the town name Chinook, Montana, which is near the Canadian border. The token itself is from a railroad that was serviced by the Minnesota & Northwestern Railroad (“M.&N.W.R.R.”) as well as the St. Paul, Minneapolis, and Manitoba Railway Company (“StP.M&M.RY.”). The token would have been used as a receipt for checked baggage along one of the lines. As neither line appears to have passed through Chinook, it is impossible to say where Owney actually received this token.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: The locations of some of the tokens Owney received on his journeys are impossible to track down. This circular metal token is marked simply with the numbers “50” and “3” and offers no clues to its origin.

title: R.N.I. & B. Railroad baggage claim check Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/8 in. (3.81 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney probably received this token while riding on the Richmond, Nicholasville, Irving & Beattyville railroad in Kentucky. The token is a baggage check, which was given to passengers to locate their luggage that was stored in the baggage hold for the trip. The line, nicknamed the Riney B, operated from 1888 to 1902. The Riney B was named for the largest towns along its route through central Kentucky: Richmond, Irvine, Nicholasville, and Beattyville. The railroad’s carriage of mail and passengers was almost secondary to its use to bring lumber and coal across the state. The token was created by metal maker James Murdock of Cincinnati, Ohio. The back side of the token bears Murdock’s mark, noting that he was also at work as, or in, “seal presses, stamp cutting, engraver, and die sinker.”

title: Boston & Portland P.S. Packet Company Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 1 3/4 in. (4.13 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Not all of Owney’s mail-related travels were on trains. Owney received this baggage check token from a sidewheel paddle steamboat. The Steamer Tremont, operated by the Portland Steam Packet Company, carried passengers and mail between Portland, Maine and Boston, Massachusetts. This boat was known as a nightboat, traveling between the two cities overnight. The baggage token, #13, would have been used to check a piece of passenger luggage during the trip. This baggage check was made by John Robbins, who began crafting such tokens in the early 1840s in Boston, Massachusetts.

title: Kampeska House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 13/16 x 1 3/4 in. (4.6 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel room check key token for room #40 from the Kampeska House hotel in Watertown, South Dakota. During the years that Owney could have visited the hotel, it was run by Cincinatus C. Wiley, a Civil War veteran originally from Massachusetts. Owney may have arrived in Watertown on one of a number of railway lines, including the Minneapolis & St. Paul; the Northwestern; or the Burlington & Cedar Rapids.

title: Atlanta, Georgia Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 x 1 1/2 in. (3.49 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this brass shield-shaped tag on a visit to Atlanta, Georgia. The tag is dated April 8, 1892. The tag includes the initials RMS, which stands for Railway Mail Service. There is no information available to indicate who presented the tag to Owney.

title: Newberry's Bus Line Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney may have received this transportation token (“good for 1 ride”) from the “Newberry’s Bus line” of Ft. Dodge, Iowa. That bus line provided tokens for riders to and from the town’s railway station. A number of railway lines passed through Ft. Dodge, including the Illinois Central, the Chicago, Rock Island, and Pacific, and the Mason City and Fort Dodge lines.

title: Atlantic & Pacific Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 1/2 in. (3.18 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check token while aboard an Atlantic & Pacific Railroad mail car. The railway’s title was a bit of a misnomer. The railroad was operated in two separate segments, neither of which touched on the Atlantic coast. One segment ran between St. Louis, Missouri to Tulsa, Oklahoma. The second segment ran from Albuquerque, New Mexico into California. The local marking indicates that the passenger and baggage would have traveled only on this line, not onto a connecting one. This baggage check token was created by William W. Wilcox, a Chicago-based manufacturer.

title: Oregon and California Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (4.45 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney would have received this baggage check token while on the Oregon and California Railroad. The O&C began in Oregon and operated from 1869-1972, although the line did not cross the California border until 1887, a year before Owney began his travels. This baggage check token was created by William W. Wilcox, a Chicago-based manufacturer.

title: Yellowstone Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney’s travels may have taken him to Yellowstone National Park, but as far as is known by his tokens, this may be as close as he got to that famous area. He probably received this hotel key token while visiting the Yellowstone Hotel in Glendive, Montana. The town is located near the border of Montana and North Dakota. The town was a stop along the Northern Pacific Railroad during Owney’s lifetime. The token itself was manufactured by “NW Stamp Works,” a northwest company that also manufactured police badges, rubber stamps for city offices, date stamps, and dog license tokens.

title: O'Connor's Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 3/4 x 2 1/4 in. (6.99 x 5.72 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token while visiting O’Connor’s Hotel in Winnipeg, Canada. Owney made at least one trip to Winnipeg during his lifetime, in the summer of 1895, just a month before he started off on his journey around the world.

title: Naugatuck Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/4 in. (3.81 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check token from someone along the Naugatuck Railroad. The Naugatuck operated in Connecticut as a connecting line from the New York & New Haven RR. It merged with that company in 1906. This baggage check was made by John Robbins, who began crafting such tokens in the early 1840s in Boston, Massachusetts.

title: Vancouver Hotel Owney tag
places: British Columbia & Vancouver Island (British colony; Canadian pr
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 13/16 x 1 1/2 in. (4.6 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel baggage check token while visiting the Vancouver Hotel in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. The hotel operated from 1887-1916. Owney is known to have made at least a half dozen trips across the border into Canada during his lifetime. The date Owney received this token is undetermined, but it is known that visited the area in 1895. Another famous world traveler, Mark Twain, stayed at the same hotel in mid August 1895 while on a lecture tour. There is no evidence the two ever crossed paths, but the hotel was evidently the choice for world travelers, human and canine alike.

title: Columbia House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 13/16 x 1 1/2 in. (4.6 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token from a hotel known as “Columbia House.” Even though the proprietor’s name, W. Bohn, is known, there is not yet any information on where or when the dog received this trinket.

title: Guichon Hotel Owney tag
places: British Columbia & Vancouver Island (British colony; Canadian pr
dimensions: Height x Width: 4 13/16 x 3 1/2 in. (12.22 x 8.89 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token while on a trip into Canada. The token would have been used to identify the key to room #32 at the Guichon Hotel in North Westminster, British Columbia, now a suburb of Vancouver, British Columbia. The dog probably arrived in town along the Canadian Pacific Railway in the early 1890s.

title: Owney tag marked R.H.
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: This brass octagonal tag is marked with the initials R.H. and the number "2." There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, who presented it, or where.

title: Station G Brooklyn, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1/8 x 2 1/4 in. (0.32 x 5.72 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while visiting Brooklyn, New York in early April 1894. The token is dated “Apr. 12 -94” on the back and the front indicates Owney’s visit was to the Station G Brooklyn post office. According to the Brooklyn Daily Eagle Almanac from 1891, Station G served a district from “the East River and Newtown Creek along creek to Meeker Avenue, to Richardson Street, to Union Avenue, to North 14th, to East River.” The Brooklyn Daily Eagle newspaper from April 9, 1894 recorded Owney’s arrival in the area. In the story with a playful headline, “Inspector Owney Here,” the paper refers to the dog as “a visitor of national reputation,” and recorded his visit to the main Brooklyn post office, where he was welcomed by Postmaster Andrew T. Sullivan.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 2 1/8 in. (2.54 x 5.4 cm)
descriptions: There is no definitive information that indicates where or when Owney received this token. The names G. Grafton and H. McGowan do not appear in the same post office together in any of the US registers of the Post Office Department during the 1890s.

title: South Dakota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while traveling in South Dakota. The item is an advertisement for Black Hills tin. During the early 1890s, the area experienced a boom in Black Hills tin, but by 1893 the boom had gone bust. The token, made from Black Hills tin, is engraved with the words “In the spirit of love and justice the people rule.” It is not known who gave the token to Owney, or where in South Dakota he may have received it.

title: Holly Springs Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 7/8 x 1 3/4 in. (4.76 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token from the Holly Springs Hotel in Holly Springs, Mississippi. The token, which would have been used for room key #22, indicates that the hotel was possibly owned by the Illinois Central railroad. That railroad, along with the Kansas, Memphis, and Birmingham, passed through the town of Holly Springs. The hotel was located near at the train tracks, and would have been used by traveling railway mail clerks as well as regular railway employees.

title: Banner Division Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while visiting Cincinnati, Ohio on April 11, 1892. There is no additional information to identify the “Banner Division 5th” identified on the front portion of the token. The back has an engraver’s mark from James Murdock Jr., a Cincinnati engraver and metals manufacturer.

title: H. J. Thyes Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token from Herman J. Thyes, who worked as a liquor salesman in Reno, Nevada in the 1890s. Thyes produced a series of such tokens during his business career. Trade checks such as these were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases. This token offered the owner “one drink or cigar” on one side, with a list of products for sale on the other. At some point in his career Thyes was the proprietor of The Crystal saloon on 2nd Street in Reno.

title: Hotel Claremont Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 × 1 5/8 in. (4.13 × 4.13 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token while visiting the Hotel Claremont in Claremont, New Hampshire. There is no additional information available on when Owney received the token. The three-story hotel was designed by William Ralph Emerson, a cousin of the famous writer, Ralph Waldo Emerson. The hotel was located on the northern side of Tremont Square and was built in 1892.

title: US Mail Service Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 4 in. (4.13 x 10.16 cm)
descriptions: There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney. The identity of the donor and the location are also unknown. The tag is labeled U.S. Mail Service, with those words surrounding the number "5." The shape of the tag is similar to the identification badges used by Rural Free Delivery (RFD) carriers. The RFD badges were not issued by the Post Office Department but could be purchased by manufacturers who sold directly to rural carriers.

title: Lancaster House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag when he visited the Lancaster House in Lancaster, New Hampshire, on May 5, 1896. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Fond du Lac, Wisconsin Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 3 in. (3.81 x 7.62 cm)
descriptions: Owney probably received this token from a representative of Harrison’s manufacturing business. A former postal employee, Harrison partnered with William P. Towne, forming the Charles Harrison & Company manufacturers of brass and plumbers’ supplies in Fond du Lac, Wisconsin. In 1890, the company ran into financial difficulties. Harrison managed to continue producing products, including the “mail distributing rack” that is advertised on this token. He patented the rack on April 8, 1879, patent #214,036. Harrison’s “system of mail-car fixtures and furniture of portable drop-tables and bag racks” had the welfare of the Railway Mail Service clerks in mind. It was designed to “more fully utilize the space, admit light from the windows, secure better ventilation, economize time, facilitate work, lessen the number and individual labor of clerks.” Harrison made the mail racks his life’s work. In the 1900 census, at age 77, Harrison listed his occupation as “Manufactures Postal Racks.”

title: Hotel Seagrave Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 5/8 in. (5.08 x 4.13 cm)
descriptions: Owney probably received this hotel key check token from Arthur A. Seagrave or one of his employees. Sometime in 1889-1890, Seagrave built a hotel on the corner of Virginia and 3rd Avenue in Seattle, Washington, naming it after himself. Owney was either a regular or popular guest at the hotel, for he received not one, but two hotel key check tokens from the Seagrave, both for room #12. While it is not known when Owney received this token, Arthur Seagrave opened a new hotel, the Occidental, sometime before 1893.

title: Hotel Seagrave Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 5/8 in. (5.08 x 4.13 cm)
descriptions: Owney probably received this hotel key check token from Arthur A. Seagrave or one of his employees. Sometime in 1889-1890, Seagrave built a hotel on the corner of Virginia and 3rd Avenue in Seattle, Washington, naming it after himself. Owney was either a regular or popular guest at the hotel, for he received not one, but two hotel key check tokens from the Seagrave, both for room #12. While it is not known when Owney received this token, Arthur Seagrave opened a new hotel, the Occidental, sometime before 1893.

title: T.P. & B. T. Co. Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 13/16 x 1 1/2 in. (4.6 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check token from a transportation company with the initials “TP & BT.“ There is no additional information to indicate the name of the company, when or where it was given to the dog. The token was manufactured by William W. Wilcox’s manufacturing company. Based in Chicago, Wilcox’s company produced a number of baggage check tokens during Owney’s lifetime.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: There is little information that explains when, where, or from whom Owney received this token. The token itself was manufactured by James Murdock Jr. of Cincinnati, Ohio. Murdock advertised himself as a “Stamp Cutter, Engraver and Die Sinker.” The token is similar in shape and style to baggage check tokens that Murdock produced. The initials S.E.P. and the number 9 remain a mystery.

title: Tacoma, Washington Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
descriptions: Among Owney’s more unusual tokens is this one given to him from the Tacoma [Washington] Poultry Association. The association held a show between December 31, 1895 and January 4, 1896, and quite possibly Owney was visiting the city at that time. Given Owney’s demonstrated fondness for chasing chickens, it is hard to imagine he would have behaved himself at a poultry show. Just two years earlier Owney had rewarded a California clerk’s hospitality by chasing the family’s chickens. By the time the clerk responded to the wild cackling and squawking in his yard, Owney was found with the “finest and largest fowl of the yard” in his mouth.
Reference:
Los Angeles Times, “Owney’s ‘Fowl’ Crime,” April 30, 1893, p. 7.

title: Detroit, Michigan Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 2 1/2 in. (5.72 x 6.35 cm)
descriptions: This metal shield-shaped tag was given to Owney on his visit to Detroit, Michigan, on November 11, 1893. Just as Owney’s presence in a city was an opportunity to interest the local press in an unusual story, Owney was a walking billboard for civic organizations and store owners. Owney’s Detroit tag advertised the city as the “Beautiful City of the Straits” to those who met the dog after his visit there.

title: US Post Office Department Washington, D.C. Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 × 2 1/8 in. (5.4 × 5.4 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the postal workers whose jobs were to repair the thousands of mailbags and mail locks that were damaged during service. Given the purported love of Owney for the smell of mailbags, this shop would have been a necessary stop. The token notes that it was presented to Owney on April 13, 1892. At that time, the Washington, DC repair shop was the center of Department’s bag and lock repair work. Superintendent Franklin B. Kirkbridge managed a shop of 230 workers (120 men; 110 women) located at 479 and 481 C Street, NW. The five-story tall building held workers who repaired and returned into service 200,000 mailbags each month.

Of the workers who were employed at the repair shop, women were employed for the most part in piece work on the jute canvas sacks. They sewed the bags, repaired and restrung them as needed at the rate of 3 1/2 cents per bag. They were expected to finish 38 bags each day. The male workers were paid by the month, $75 a month for leather and canvas workers; $50 a month for the laborers who received, shook out, handled, packed, and reshipped the bags after they had been repaired.

title: 2nd Division RMS Superintendent's office Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3 × 3 in. (7.62 × 7.62 cm)
descriptions: Owney (or Owenie, as this token’s donors spelled his name) received this trinket from the office of Richard C. Jackson, Second Division Superintendent of the Railway Mail Service in New York City. The token notes the special relationship between the dog and the nation’s Railway Mail Service employees, noting that he was a “faithful friend.” There is no notation on the token indicating when it was presented to the traveler. Owney visited New York City on a regular basis during his lifetime, and he could have received it almost anytime during his lifetime.

title: George Anderson Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 x 1 5/16 in. (2.22 x 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token while visiting Omaha, Nebraska. The token sports the name of George Anderson, and his position as a clerk in the post office at Omaha. The back of the token is dated 1892. Anderson, a Scottish immigrant, worked as a clerk for several years before transferring over to Omaha’s Free City Delivery service as a letter carrier. Tokens such as these were often attached to keys or luggage in case they were lost.

title: J.H. Dwyer's Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token good for “10 cents” or “one cigar” from James H. Dwyer’s store in Cross, Oklahoma (the town was located just a few miles south of present day Kildare, Oklahoma). The there is no additional information to indicate when the token was given to Owney. Cross was located along the Santa Fe railroad line.

title: Topham's Trunk Depot luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 × 2 1/4 in. (4.45 × 5.72 cm)
descriptions: Owney received some leather baggage identification tags during his travels. This tag was manufactured by Topham’s Trunks of Washington, D.C. As the tag indicates, the Topham shop was located at that time at 231 Pennsylvania Avenue S.E. in Washington, D.C.

title: Santa Cruz, California luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token good for “one drink” while visiting the Pacific Ocean House hotel and saloon in Santa Cruz, California. This is a “trade check,” a token that was “good for” free items, or a few cents off of a product. This token also notes that E.J. Swift was the proprietor of the hotel. Swift had passed away by 1892, at a time when Owney was still in the early years of his travels. It is unknown when Owney received this token, but it may likely have been after Swift’s death.

title: St. Charles Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token, probably a hotel key check token, from an establishment called the “St. Charles.” During Owney’s lifetime, several towns had hotels and rooming establishments called St. Charles and there is no additional information to indicate when or where the token was given to the dog.

title: Luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 x 2 3/4 in. (5.4 x 6.99 cm)
descriptions: In addition to hundreds of metal tokens, Owney received some leather baggage tags. This weathered tag does not include any information that would indicate who gave it to Owney, or when and where the tag was placed among the dog’s treasures.

title: Luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 3 in. (4.13 x 7.62 cm)
descriptions: In addition to hundreds of metal tokens, Owney received some leather baggage tags. The tag is in relatively good condition, but the owner’s identification information is missing from the “window” cut into one side of the tag. Without it, there is nothing to indicate who gave the tag to Owney, or when and where it was given to the dog.

title: Alfred V. Friedrich luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 7/8 x 1 1/4 in. (4.76 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: In addition to hundreds of metal tokens, Owney received some leather tags. This tag was produced by Alfred V. Friedrich. Friedrich owned a shoe store in Traverse City, Michigan and was named the town’s postmaster on March 1, 1891. Among the railway lines that passed through Traverse City during Owney’s lifetime were the Michigan Central, the Chicago & West Michigan and Grand Rapids & Indian railroads.

title: S.E. Bovee El Paso, Texas luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 3 1/8 in. (5.08 x 7.94 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this leather baggage tag from Sheldon E. Bovee on March 28, 1892. Bovee was a letter carrier in El Paso, Texas. El Paso was a stop along the Southern and the Atchison, Topeka and the Santa Fe railroads.

title: Union News luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/2 x 2 1/8 in. (6.35 x 5.4 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this leather baggage tag advertising the “Union News,” owned by the Union News Company. The company contracted with railroads across the country to sell its newspapers in railroad stations and aboard railway trains. Owney would have come across many copies of the company’s newspaper in his travels.

title: J. R. Monfort & Co. luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5 1/2 x 2 5/8 in. (13.97 x 6.67 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this leather tag from James A. Smith of El Paso, Texas. Smith served as the town’s postmaster from June 1890 to January 1894. The tag also bears the name of the maker, “J.R. Montford & Co.” also of El Paso. During Owney’s lifetime El Paso was a stop along the Southern and the Atchison, Topeka and the Santa Fe railroads.

title: Henry Freudenberger luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 3 1/8 in. (5.08 × 7.94 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this leather luggage tag from the manufacturing firm of Henry Freudenberger. Freudenberger manufactured and sold trunks and valises in Cincinnati, Ohio. A number of names are listed on the front side of the tag (where the luggage owner’s address would be placed), including W.E. Austin and J.E. Diefe. Owney visited Cincinnati a number of times during his lifetime.

title: Luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 3 1/4 in. (5.72 x 8.26 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this leather luggage tag from a group of postal clerks on May 15, 1896. The clerks marked their gift on the front side of the tag where the luggage owner’s address would be placed. In addition to noting that the tag was from “postal clerks” they added a wish of “good luck to Owney” to their gift. There is no additional information to indicate where this tag was given to the dog.

title: Luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 3 in. (4.13 x 7.62 cm)
descriptions: In addition to hundreds of metal tokens, Owney received some leather baggage tags. The tag is in relatively good condition, but the owner’s identification information is missing from the “window” cut into one side of the tag. Without it, there is nothing to indicate who gave the tag to Owney, or when and where it was given to the dog.

title: Young's Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 3 1/4 in. (5.72 x 8.26 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check tag from Young’s Hotel of Franklin Falls (now known simply as Franklin), New Hampshire. The hotel was owned and operated by Robert Young. There is no additional information indicating when the tag was given to Owney.

title: Luggage Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 3 3/4 in. (5.08 x 9.53 cm)
descriptions: In addition to hundreds of metal tokens, Owney received some leather baggage tags. The tag is in relatively good condition, but the owner’s identification information is missing from the “window” cut into one side of the tag. Without it, there is nothing to indicate who gave the tag to Owney, or when and where it was given to the dog.

title: Fraser Canyon House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 x 1 1/2 in. (3.49 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token during one of his visits to Canada. The Fraser Canyon House was a hotel located in North Bend, north of Vancouver, British Columbia. There is no additional information on the token to indicate when it was presented to the dog.

title: The Tacoma Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney obtained this hotel key check token while visiting The Tacoma Hotel in Tacoma, Washington. The hotel, built by architect Stanford White in 1884, drew a number of remarkable guests, including writer Mark Twain. In the early 1890s the hotel had its own mascot, an 800-pound bear named Jack. There are no records that reveal if the two mascots ever met, and perhaps the hotel staff wisely kept them well separated during Owney’s visit.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token during his travels. The item bears the number 40. There is no information to indicate when or where Owney received the token, or who presented it to the dog.

title: Third Division RMS Washington, D.C. Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 3 in. (5.08 x 7.62 cm)
descriptions: Postal employees under the direction of Charles W. Vickery, Third Division Superintendent of the Railway Mail Service, presented this token to Owney on April 18, 1892. The token, cut in the shape of a postal badge, celebrates the link between the Railway Mail Service and their canine mascot.

title: Trainmen's House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)

names.label: Associated Railroad
names.content: New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad, 1872 - 1968

descriptions: Owney received this hotel check key from the “Trainman’s House” in New Haven, Connecticut. A number of railway companies, including the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad, owned hotels along their rail lines. The title indicates that this particular hotel was intended primarily for the company’s railway employees, as well as the Railway Mail Service postal clerks who were also working the trains that passed through. The token was manufactured by Hoole Manufacturing Company of New York. Edmund Hoole had a small manufacturing company that produced baggage and key check tokens. In 1893 his company was purchased by the American Railway Supply Company.

title: F. J. Morgan Bald Knob, Arkansas Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from F.J. Morgan of Bald Knob, Arkansas. The tag is dated 1888, which is the year that Owney was first associated with the Albany post office. It is likely that Mr. Morgan already owned this tag with the date on it and gave it to Owney when the dog began traveling into some southern states. Morgan was a railway office telegrapher who worked along the Missouri Pacific Railway line.

title: Railroad Eating House & Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3 × 3 in. (7.62 × 7.62 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token from a railway hotel most probably located in Tracy, California. There is no information on the token to indicate when he received it. Owney made a number of trips to and through California, first visiting the state in April 1891. Some of Owney’s hotel key check tokens are from visits to large exquisitely decorated hotels, the finest of their cities. But for Owney, and his Railway Mail Service companions, the more likely accommodations would be a small hotel or boarding house near the train station. This token represents the latter, with the very apt and descriptive title of “Railroad Eating House & Hotel.”

title: Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 2 in. (4.45 x 5.08 cm)
descriptions: This tag marks Owney’s travels on a branch line of the Cincinnati, Hamilton and Dayton railway. Ainslie and Phyllis Carter of Cincinnati, Ohio presented this tag to Owney on September 5, 1894.

title: Puyallup, Washington Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 × 2 1/4 in. (5.72 × 5.72 cm)
descriptions: This round brass tag was given to Owney to wish him good luck on the beginning of his around-the-world journey. Owney left from Tacoma, Washington, on August 19, 1895. The names of eleven men and women decorate the tag. Those wishing Owney good luck with this tag were Mrs. R. H. Coffman, Glen C. Elvins, F.T.C. Myers, W.F. Adams, C.A. McLaughlin, Frank McAlpin, Herman Klaber, Thomas McNeff, and Charles Hood of nearby Puyallup, Washington. The tag is dated August 14, 1895.

title: Windsor Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 2 5/8 × 3 3/8 × 1/16 in. (6.67 × 8.57 × 0.16 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token from a hotel named Windsor. There is no additional information to indicate when or where the dog received this tag. During Owney’s lifetime, there were a number of locations with hotels named Windsor, including a number cities that Owney is known to have visited, such as: New York City, Denver, Colorado, and Montreal, Canada.

title: Nashville, Tennessee Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 2 in. (4.45 x 5.08 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this shield-shaped metal tag on April 9, 1892, while visiting Nashville, Tennessee. The tag was imprinted by Southern Rubber Stamp Works of Nashville. While the tag is labeled Railway Mail Service and is shaped like a badge, it was not an actual RMS badge.

title: Fort Wayne, Indiana Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 1/4 × 2 1/2 × 1/2 in. (3.18 × 6.35 × 1.27 cm)
descriptions: This item is unique among the tokens Owney received during his lifetime. The decorative spoon bowl was given to Owney in Ft. Wayne, Indiana. The bowl of the spoon is decorated with a scene of the fort, originally constructed in 1794 and named for General Anthony Wayne. The convex side reads notes that it is from the Ft. Wayne post office department, and presented to Owney on March 27, 1894. During Owney’s lifetime, Ft. Wayne was a stop or transfer point for a number of railway lines, including the Evansville & Richmond and Evansville & Terre Haute lines; the Pittsburgh, Cincinnati, Chicago & St. Louis Railroad; as well as the Cleveland, Cincinnati, Chicago, and St. Louis Railroad. The Grand Trunk Western and the Chicago & Eastern Illinois Railroads may also have carried Owney into Ft. Wayne.

title: Baltimore, Maryland Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 7/8 x 1 7/8 x 1/8 in. (4.76 x 4.76 x 0.32 cm)
descriptions: This Maltese cross-shaped metal tag was presented to Owney by the staff or proprietors of Crowl & Lehner, a company that supplied postmarking and other stamping devices. The company was located in Baltimore, Maryland. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Jackson, Mississippi Post Office Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 3 1/8 x 7/8 x 1/8 in. (7.94 x 2.22 x 0.32 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag during a trip to Jackson, Mississippi. The tag is inscribed on one side by postal clerk William Henry Gibbs Jr., and on the other side by E.H. Dunning, also of Jackson, Mississippi. While Gibbs’ name is listed in the official registrar of postal employees of that era, Dunning is not. His connection to the Post Office Department is unknown. A number of railway lines ran through Jackson at that time, including the Illinois Central; the Yazoo & Mississippi Valley; the New Orleans & North Eastern; and the Memphis & Charleston Railroads.

title: Baltimore and Grafton Railway Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 7/8 x 1 1/2 in. (4.76 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: This horseshoe-shaped metal tag includes the inscription that it was presented to “His Dogship by F.M.Parker.” The reverse of the tag includes the date April 20, 1892, and the railway line, the Baltimore and Grafton Railway Post Office (RPO) car.

title: Corry, Pennsylvania Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/16 x 1 3/4 in. (5.24 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: This tag was presented to Owney while visiting Corry, Pennsylvania. The tag is marked for the A & CW railway. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Half Dollar Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: There is no information that reveals when, where, or from whom Owney received this coin. The half dollar, minted in Philadelphia, has not one, but four holes drilled into it.

title: Charleston, West Virginia Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 3/4 in. (3.18 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney was a dog who became the unofficial mascot of the Railway Mail Service in the late 19th century. At some point in his travels, Railway Post Office clerks and postmasters began to attach mementoes to the dog’s collar. The steadily growing collection of tags included claim tags, hotel key tags, tokens, badges, medals, coins, buttons and other trinkets.

This tag is unique in the Owney collection. It is the only one that represents what was carried in the hundreds of mailbags that Owney followed from train to train. It is shaped like an envelope, with an address, stamp, and even a canceling mark etched on one side. The envelope is addressed to Wm. Jones of Charleston, West Virginia, who is identified as a letter carrier. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Albuquerque Railroad Post Office Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 7/8 x 1 1/2 in. (4.76 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while visiting “the City of Sunshine,” Albuquerque, New Mexico. The token was obtained from someone working on the La J. & aAlbuquerque post office. There is no additional information to indicate when the token was given to the dog.

title: Grand Rapids, Michigan Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: A few of the tags Owney received during his travels were originally meant for dogs. This license tag, number 1077 from Grand Rapids, Michigan, indicated payment for a dog license in 1895.

title: Baltimore, Maryland Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 × 2 1/4 in. (5.72 × 5.72 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this specially designed token from National Association of Post Office Clerks during their third national convention in Baltimore, Maryland. The tag is dated April 19, 1892, three years to the day before Owney would set out on his around the world journey. The clerks were appreciative fans of the dog early in his traveling career.

title: Charlestown, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 × 2 1/8 in. (5.4 × 5.4 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from a visit to Charlestown, Massachusetts. The round brass tag notes that Owney “called on” Dan Kelly’s grocery store on June 22, 1894.

title: Brooklyn, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 2 1/2 in. (1.91 x 6.35 cm)
descriptions: On occasion, people presented Owney with tags that dogs would naturally have, such as this one from Brooklyn, New York. It is a dog license tag, number 5758. The date, 1891, indicates it may be one of the earliest tags in the collection. There is no indication whether it was presented to Owney then or whether the tag was left over from an earlier year.

title: Jackson, Mississippi Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: The design of this oval-shaped, metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. This one is marked "Wilson Parker, I.C.L. Counter, Jackson, Miss." There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Buffalo, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Postal workers at the Buffalo, New York, post office presented this round brass tag to Owney on May 24, 1893. It is one of the earliest tags in Owney’s collection. At first, Owney did not travel far from home, including this May trip.

title: Boston, Providence and NY Night Express Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 3/4 x 2 in. (6.99 x 5.08 cm)
descriptions: W.J. Tilley of the Boston, Providence, and New York City night mail train welcomed Owney to the train car with this tag, which is dated April 27, 1892.

title: Winona, Minnesota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: This brass, triangular-shaped key was presented to Owney at Winona, Minnesota. The tag carries the date June 16, 1895, on the back.

title: Lawrence, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 2 in. (2.54 x 5.08 cm)
descriptions: While visiting Lawrence, Massachusetts, Owney received this brass oval tag from George H. Leck’s photography studio. The tag includes the phrase “I had my Photo taken there.” If Owney did have a photograph taken at Leck’s studio, there is no known record of it.

title: Haverhill, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from a creative person in Haverhill, Massachusetts. The specially made token is inscribed with a poem, “This tag will tell you all the news; Owney has visited the city of shoes” and is dated June 16, 1894. There is no information on who gave this tag to the dog. This is one of several promotional tags given to Owney, treating the dog as something of a traveling advertisement.

title: Nashville, Tennessee Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 1/2 in. (2.54 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: From time to time, Owney received tokens for goods on his journeys. This square brass token was redeemable for one quart of milk. It is undetermined whether the stamped letters "R.C.C." refer to a business. On the reverse side of the metal piece, someone etched: "Nashville, Tenn / Tom Glascock." According to census records from the time of Owney's travels, William J. Glascock, father of Thomas M. Glascock born 1874 in Tennessee, worked for railway mail and the family were living Tennessee around 1891 according to a voter registration list. (They were also listed in the 1880 Census in Fulton County, Georgia, where William Glascock worked for railway mail). There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, but it is conceivable that someone carved young Tom's name into the metal piece, perhaps when William, Tom, and other family members of the Glascock family may have met Owney while William worked with the railway mail.

title: Louisville, Kentucky Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 in. (2.54 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: This octagon-shaped metal tag has markings on both sides. The front identifies it as having come from the Commonwealth Life Insurance Company of Louisville, Kentucky. The back proclaims the company’s motto, “United We Stand, Divided We Fall, A Square Deal for Every Policy Holder” with an image of two men shaking hands. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Louisville, Kentucky Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: This token from a Louisville, Kentucky, store is marked “good for 5 cents trade or cash” at D.C. Brenner & Company. The company advertises its wears as including rubber stamps, stencils, seas, pool mining, and hotel checks. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Herber W. Hull Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 in. (3.18 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from Heber W. Hull of Plymouth, New Hampshire. Hull was a railroad employee and not associated with the Post Office Department. This tag notes Hull’s employer at the time, the Concord & Montreal Railroad. By 1905 Hull was working as a conductor for the C&M Railroad’s owner, the Boston & Maine Railroad. In addition to working for the railroads, Hull was a Mason. The circular symbol with the initials KSHTWSST notes that Hull was a Royal Arch Mason and Master Mason in his local lodge.

title: Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this pedal-shaped token from the Stag in Cincinnati. There is no additional information indicating when Owney received this tag. The Stag was a hotel as well as a saloon. The Stag saloon was owned by Tony Honing and Edwin W. Baylis. The hotel was advertised as “for gentlemen only” and as a “handy hotel popular with country merchants and commercial travelers” and was managed by Walter H. Maxwell.

title: J.F.C. Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
descriptions: There is little information to indicate when or where Owney received this tag. It seems to have been given to him by an individual with the initials J.F.C. of Princeton, Indiana. The tag is marked on both sides with the notation K of H, or Knights of Honor, a lodge founded in 1873.

title: Hornellsville, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 x 1 3/8 in. (3.49 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this decorated tag from Mason L. Wafer of Hornellsville, New York. There is no information indicating when Owney received the tag. Wafer was a business owner according to the 1891 Steuben County directory, but his business is not listed. If the illustration is any indication, it may well have been related to roller skating. Owney received two tags from this city’s businessmen. The other came from Fred D. Lockwood, a clerk in his father’s shoemaking business. Hornellsville was on at least two railway lines that Owney traveled, the New York & Erie and the Buffalo and New York City lines.

title: Hotel Fife Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel check key tag from the Hotel Fife in Tacoma, Washington. The five-story hotel, built in 1888, was located on the northwest corner of 9th and Pacific and was torn down in 1925. William H. Fife, the hotel’s owner, was born in Ontario, Canada. He was an important figure in the early days of Tacoma, building the first general store and acting as the city’s first postmaster (1874-1882) and became one of the city’s most prosperous citizens.

The tag itself was produced by the Talcott Brothers, who owned a jewelry business in Olympia, Washington, as is noted at the top portion of the tag. Lucius Ford Talcot and his son, Charles established the first business. Charles’ brothers George and Lucius Grant Talcott continued the work as the Talcott Brothers. The business thrived and grew, with the store selling more than just jewelry (bicycles and sewing machines, among other items). In 1889 the trio were asked to design the Washington state seal.

title: St. Paul & A. Lea Railway Post Office Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from an individual whose name appears to be Frank R. Hedrick of Chaska, Minnesota. The official Post Office Department registers of the time do not list any postal or railway mail service workers by that name during Owney’s travels. There is no additional information from the tag to indicate Hedrick’s connection to the Department.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: There is no information associated with this tag to indicate when or where Owney received it, nor from whom. The only markings on the tags are the letter G, A, and F.

title: J.P. Palmer Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification tag from J.P. Palmer of New York City, New York. There is no information on the tag to indicate when it was given to the dog, nor Palmer’s profession. The official registers of the Post Office Department for the 1890s do not list a J.P. Palmer in any New York postal facility.

title: Knights of the Grip Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 2 1/2 in. (5.08 x 6.35 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from a Michigan state association known as the “Knights of the Grip.” The group, an organization of traveling salesmen, was well known to railway employees, including postal clerks. The suitcase-shaped tag was the symbol of the group. Michigan’s “Knights of the Grip” allowed membership from anyone who “has been employed for the term of a year or more as a traveling man, and not over 50 years of age. In good health, not afflicted with any chronic disease, and not addicted to the use of intoxicating liquors as a beverage, residing or traveling in the State of Michigan.” Aside from the requirements that a member be a traveling “man” the traveling railway mail dog may well have been seen as a fellow knight by the salesmen.

title: Central Fire Station Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received a handful of tags from firemen and fire stations around the country, including this tag representing Lowell, Massachusetts’s Central Fire Station. There is no information on when Owney received the tag. A number of railway lines passed through Lowell, including the Boston & Main and the Old Colony Railroad. The back of the tag notes that C.O.A. Grover, a Lowell steel letter cutter, created the tag.

title: Boston & Albany Railway Post Office Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
descriptions: There is no information on when Owney received this tag, but it came from his friends in the Railway Mail Service. The tag notes that it was given by clerks of the Boston & Albany railway line, specifically those working in the Railway Post Office trains #5 and #12. The phrase “Always welcome on the no longer gilt edge” may be a reference to the usually reliably profitable Boston & Albany enduring a bad year.

title: Howard Young Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 1/4 in. (2.54 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification tag from Howard Young of St. Paul, Minnesota. Young worked as a brakeman for the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis, & Omaha railway. The tag is also inscribed “F.L.T.,” or Friendship, Love and Truth, a signifier of the fraternal organization known as the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. There is no information on the tag to indicate when Owney may have received it.

title: Pontiac, Illinois Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 in. (1.91 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check tag from Silas A. Rathbun, a Pontiac, Illinois businessman and active member of the state’s Democratic Party. Trade checks such as these were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases. This token offered the owner 25-cents off of a purchase of furniture in Rathbun’s Dry Goods store (which he later developed into a Department Store). Rathbun also served as the city’s mayor for a number of years (1889-1901, 1903-1905, and 1911-1913). There is no additional information on when this tag was given to Owney, but Rathbun’s first term as mayor overlapped the years of Owney’s travels. Thus, in the town of Pontiac, Illinois, Owney was greeted by the town mayor.

title: Postmaster William W. Johnson Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 in. (3.18 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from William W. Johnson who served as Baltimore’s postmaster from 1890-1894. The shield-shaped tag includes a recognizable piece of the Baltimore landscape, the Washington Monument in Mt. Vernon square.

title: F.D. Lockwood Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from Fred D. Lockwood of Hornellsville, New York. The tag is one of two Owney received from businessmen in that city. The other was from Mason L. Wafer, whose business may have been related to the roller skating industry. Lockwood was a clerk in his father’s shoemaking business. Hornellsville was on at least two railway lines that Owney traveled, the New York & Erie and the Buffalo and New York City lines.

title: George A. Reinville Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification tag from George A. Reinville, who is listed in the Manchester, New Hampshire city directories as first a clerk at an unidentified business on Merrimack Street, then a janitor at Union Depot. The tag notes that Mr. Reinville was a member of the Ancient Order of Foresters, a fraternal society rooted in England. The back of the tag is engraved with “Bakersville N.H.” and the initials “K.S. F.,” which may stand for the Knights of St. Francis.

title: Portland, Maine Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: The design of this oval-shaped, metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. The staff or proprietors at Lane & Collins, photographers at the Portland, Maine, railway station gave this tag to Owney. The tag indicates that Owney visited the station and studio on April 14, 1896.

title: Seattle, Washington Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hand engraved tag during a visit to Seattle, Washington, on July 17, 1895. Owney made a number of trips to the Seattle / Tacoma area, including August 1895, when he started out on his around the world tour. There is no information to indicate who presented this tag to the dog.

title: E.D. Simpson Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney was given this identification tag by E.D. Simpson of Running Water, South Dakota. The tag is dated 1893. There is no one by that name who worked for the Post Office Department during Owney’s lifetime, and no additional information that points to Mr. Simpson’s profession. The city of Running Water was served by the Chicago & Milwaukee Railway line.

title: Kansas City, Missouri Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: From time to time Owney received practical gifts for his collar--dog tags. This one, from Kansas City, Missouri, is dated 1893 and shows that someone has covered Owney’s dog tax, permitting the pooch to wander the city without fear of arrest. There is no additional information to indicate who gave this tag to Owney. Kansas City was a railway hub, served by dozens of lines. Owney undoubtedly spent a great deal of time traveling through or wandering in the city.

title: Railway Mail Service Superintendent Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 × 1 3/4 in. (4.45 × 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney’s best friends among postal employees were the railway mail clerks who rode with him on trains. While in Boston, Massachusetts, Owney often spent time visiting not only the general city post office, but also the Railway Mail Service offices. At the time of this visit, the Division Superintendent of the RMS for Boston was Edward J. Ryan, who had started his career as a railway mail service clerk in 1868, riding the Boston and Albany Railway Post Office for $1,400 a year. The pride of the Railway Mail Service workers is evident in their boast of being “First in Everything” on this tag.

title: Council Bluffs, Iowa Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: From time to time Owney received practical gifts for his collar – dog tags. This one, Council Bluffs, Iowa shows that someone has covered Owney’s dog tax in 1893, permitting the pooch to wander the city without fear of arrest. There is no additional information to indicate who gave this tag to Owney.

title: Washington DC City Post Office Owney tag
descriptions: Owney received this tag from the Washington, DC city post office on April 13, 1892. The badge was given to the dog by the Registry (or Registered Mail) Division of the local post office. The badge-shaped token was created by William F. Lutz of 626 G Street, NW, a Prussian-born engraver.

title: George W. Cooley Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from George W. Cooley, a Railway clerk who worked on the Aberdeen and Sioux City Railway line. Cooley, born in Maryland, was appointed as a mail clerk in South Dakota and was making $1,000 a year as of 1895. The tag includes the date March 19, 1894. The tag was created by Oscar J. Hoberg, a local watchmaker. Hoberg worked for James G. Thompson & Sons in Sioux City, Iowa during the time Owney was traveling. By 1900, Hoberg was able to open his own watch repair shop with George Thorpe, “Thorpe & Hoberg.”

title: Hawthorne, Nevada Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: The back side of the token is an advertisement for the Brunswick-Balke-Collender Company. Originally a billiard equipment company, Brunswick-Balke-Collender produced phonograph cases for record players.

title: San Francisco, California Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this round token while visiting San Francisco, California on April 12, 1893. The token was designed to resemble a cancellation marking, with the date “Apr 12” and time “3am” noted, as well as a “Rec’d” or received marking, noting undoubtedly the dog’s arrival. Owney was in San Francisco on his way south. On April 21, 1893, he was honored at a dog show in Los Angeles.

title: Teegarden Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 1/2 in. (5.08 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: While visiting LaPorte, Indiana, on the Northern Indiana and South Michigan Railroad, Owney received this tag from the staff or proprietor of the Teegarden Hotel. The hotel had originally been built for Dr. Abram Teegarden when the railroad first reached LaPorte in 1852. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Hotel Fife Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: The most famous of Owney’s travels was his trip around the world in the late summer and fall of 1895. That trip began and ended in Tacoma, Washington, and it may have been during one of those times that he received this hotel key tag from that city’s Fife hotel. The hotel was built by William H. Fife, a businessman who had also served for eight years as the postmaster of the city of Tacoma.

title: New Jordan House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: W. F. Jordan, the proprietor of the New Jordan House, presented this tag to Owney in honor of his visit to Brookings, South Dakota. There is no available information to indicate the date that this tag was presented to Owney. The tag was originally manufactured by W. W. Wilcox of Chicago, which was a major manufacturer of railroad baggage tags and similar metal items in the late nineteenth century. The Wilcox company produced at least two other Owney tags: 0.052985.173 and 0.052985.24.

title: The Baldwin Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: This tag was given to Owney on his visit to one of San Francisco’s most prestigious hotels, The Baldwin, which was on the corner of Powell and Market streets until it was destroyed in a fire in 1898. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Columbus, Hocking Valley & Toledo Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this metal tag when he rode train car #1583 of the Columbus, Hocking Valley and Toledo Railway Company line. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Pennsylvania and Erie Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/8 in. (3.81 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: This small metal tag was presented to Owney when he rode on the Pennsylvania and Erie Railroad, car number 7116. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Brooklyn, Bath and West End Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney obtained this round metal tag while riding in New York City. He rode the Brooklyn, Bath and West End Railroad, which had been organized in 1885 out of the Brooklyn, Bath and Coney Island Railroad. There is no information on when he rode in this car, but it was probably before the line was electrified with trolley wire in 1893. At that time, the BB & WE merged with the Atlantic Avenue Railroad.

title: Chesapeake and Ohio Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: This shield-shaped metal baggage tag was given to Owney by someone who worked along the Chesapeake and Ohio Railroad. The back of the tag indicates the agreement offered to the holder--“in consideration of free carriage of baggage, its value is agreed to be limited to one hundred dollars.” There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
