title: Philadelphia, Wilmington, and Baltimore Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag when he rode a mail car on the Philadelphia, Wilmington, and Baltimore Railroad, train car #6829. The tag also includes a marking indicating the train traveled from northeast Maryland. There is no available information to indicate the date Owney received this tag.

title: Eastern Seaboard Trip Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 in. (4.45 cm)
descriptions: This tag marks Owney’s travels on a series of small railway lines between Jersey City, New Jersey, to Jacksonville, Florida. Among the lines Owney traveled were the Pennsylvania and the Richmond, Fredericksburg and Potomac Railroad. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 1/2 in. (3.18 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag when he road on the Burlington and St. Louis portion of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad on June 22, 1895.

title: Manitoba Hall Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
descriptions: While traveling in Canada, Owney visited Winnipeg, the capitol of the Canadian province Manitoba, north of Minnesota and North Dakota. Nothing on the tag indicates how Owney traveled to Winnipeg. He might have gone on the Duluth and Winnipeg railroad. This tag marks Owney's appearance at Manitoba Hall, a large, two-story building on Portage Avenue that was, in the 1890s, the largest building in the city. There is no available information to indicate either the nature of the event held at the hall during his visit or when he received this tag.

title: San Francisco, California Owney tag
descriptions: J. Coyne of San Francisco, California, gave this metal tag to Owney. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Coat Room Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: The locations of some of the tags Owney received on his journeys are impossible to track down. This octagonal metal tag is marked simply “COATROOM 92” and offers no clues to its origin.

title: Fordham Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 1/2 in. (5.08 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this brass tag from the Fordham Hotel in Paris, Kentucky. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: San Francisco, California Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag in March 1897. On one side the name P.J. Perez is scratched in by hand, along with the location, San Francisco, California, Mission Street RPO (Railway Post Office). On the other side are printed the names J. S. Hopkins, F. J. Goslee and Evans & Pad. By 1897, Owney was quite an old dog and often ill. This tag represents his last visit to California.

title: Arlington House Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/2 x 2 in. (6.35 x 5.08 cm)
descriptions: This brass tag was given to Owney during a visit to the Arlington House hotel in Erie, Pennsylvania. There is no available information to indicate when Owney received this tag.

title: Plymouth, New Hampshire Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 x 1 5/8 in. (3.49 x 4.13 cm)
descriptions: This shield-shaped metal tag is marked “The Pemi, 58, Plymouth, NH.” The exact origin of this tag is unknown. It commemorated Owney’s trip to Plymouth, New Hampshire, and possibly a night’s stay at the city’s Pemi Hotel.

title: Paris, Kentucky Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
descriptions: This round brass medal was given to Owney by A. C. Adair, the manager of W.U.T. in Paris, Kentucky. There is currently no information on the full name of Mr. Adair’s organization.

title: Hotel Adams Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 1 1/2 in. (4.13 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: The staff or proprietor of the Hotel Adams gave Owney this tag. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney. The Hotel Adams was located in the town of Muskogee in an area then known as Indian Territory, which later became the state of Oklahoma, on the Missouri, Kansas and Texas Railroad line. The tag was originally manufactured by W. W. Wilcox of Chicago, which was a major manufacturer of railroad baggage tags and similar metal items in the late nineteenth century. At least two other Owney tags were manufactured by W.W. Wilcox: 0.052985.24, 0.052985.22, 0.052985.191, 0.052985.173, 0.052985.179, and 0.052985.156.

title: Baltimore and Grafton Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: The design of this oval-shaped, metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. George W. Ross, a Railway Post Office clerk on the Baltimore and Grafton railroad, gave this tag to Owney. There is no available information to indicate when Ross presented Owney with the tag.

title: Hotel Continental Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/8 in. (3.81 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key tag from a hotel named Continental. A number of hotels by that name existed in the US in the late 19th century. There is no available information to indicate which city’s Continental hotel this tag came from.

title: W.E.S. Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
descriptions: There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney. The small, round brass tag is labeled with the initials “W.E.S. R.R. B.M.” on one side and with the initials “R.H.” on the back.

title: Des Moines, Iowa Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
descriptions: The back side of this medal has an image of a building identified as the Iowa State Capital and seems to indicate the building’s price tag, $3,000,000.00. The front side of the medal has the image of a bearded man with the notations “Des Moines” and "September 2-3-4-5 1890.” There is no available information to indicate who presented this tag to Owney.

title: Nashville, Tennessee Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 x 2 1/2 x 1/8 in. (2.54 x 6.35 x 0.32 cm)
descriptions: C.C. Hughes, a Railway Mail Service employee from Nashville, Tennessee, gave this rectangular metal tag to Owney. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Paxton Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
descriptions: This round, metal, brass hotel key tag marked Owney’s visit to the Paxton Hotel in Omaha, Nebraska. The hotel was named for a prominent local businessman, William A. Paxton (1837-1907). There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney. The tag was originally manufactured by W. W. Wilcox, of Chicago, which was a major manufacturer of railroad baggage tags and similar metal items in the late nineteenth century. Wilcox manufactured additional baggage tags that ended-up in Owney’s possession.

title: Southern Pacific Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: This tag commemorates a trip Owney made on the Southern Pacific railroad to Sacramento, California. It’s marked "Station Porter 23." There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: This round metal tag came from Cincinnati, Ohio’s Mabley & Carew Department Store. Mabley & Carew was founded in Cincinnati in 1877 by Joseph T. Carew and C.R. Mabley. In 1881 James W. McLaughlin designed the store’s original building on Vine Street. The 12 story-tall building was demolished in 1907. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: "Good for a 5c drink" Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 × 3/4 in. (1.91 × 1.91 cm)
descriptions: Several of Owney’s tags offer him free food or drink in exchange for the tag. In this case, the tag is good for a five-cent drink. There is no information on the tag indicating where Owney needed to return to redeem the offer, nor is there any available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Pontiac, Illinois Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
descriptions: This round copper tag was presented to Owney on June 24, 1895, in Pontiac, Illinois. The tag includes the name of the Chicago and St. Louis Railway Post Office around the edges and the names “Wheeler, Googerty, Reed” in the middle.

title: Louis Cablish Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token from Edward Louis Cabish, owner of a Maysville, Kentucky, bakery. Trade checks such as these were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases. This token offered five cents off a loaf of bread. There is no information to indicate when the tag was given to Owney. Maysville, Kentucky was a frequent stop for the dog while he traveled the country.

title: Gifford House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney’s visit to Provincetown, Massachusetts, was commemorated with a circular brass room tag from the Gifford House, room 26. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Wright House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
descriptions: This circular brass tag was given to Owney while he was visiting Lancaster, Wisconsin. The tag indicates it came from the Wright House, a local three story hotel. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Lawrence, Kansas Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: The staff or proprietors of Graeber Brothers in Lawrence, Kansas, gave this donut-shaped brass tag to Owney. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, nor on the Graeber Brothers business.

title: Hannibal and St. Joseph Railway Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/4 in. (3.81 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: This Owney tag is marked for the Hannibal and St. Joseph railroad, car number 2309. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney. The Hannibal and St. Joseph railroad was the first in the nation to run a Railway Post Office sorting car, designated by Postmaster General Montgomery Blair on July 7, 1862. The service continued on the line on an experimental basis for two years.

title: Union Station Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Among Owney’s tags are several that have a direct connection with railway lines or the Railway Post Office. This metal tag is marked G. McHenry, Express No. 31, 280, Claim Baggage at Union Station. The tag was produced by Northwest Stamp Works of St. Paul, Minnesota. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Winnipeg, Manitoba Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney made at least two trips into Canada, including the one commemorated in Winnipeg, Manitoba, by this brass octagonal tag. Owney rode on a Canadian railway post office car and received this tag on June 27, 1895.

title: Kansas City, Missouri Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 3/4 in. (4.45 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this brass baggage claim check tag at the Kansas City, Missouri, Union Depot. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney. The tag was originally manufactured by W. W. Wilcox, of Chicago, which was a major manufacturer of railroad baggage tags and similar metal items in the late nineteenth century. The Wilcox company manufactured other tags that were given to Owney.

title: Running Water, Dakota Territory Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 3/4 in. (3.81 x 1.91 cm)
descriptions: The design of this oval-shaped, metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. This tag was given to Owney by F. P. Brooks of Running Water, Dakota Territory, now South Dakota. Owney would have traveled through Running Water on the Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railroad. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Champeny Brothers Store Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney could have traded this round token in for 25 cents in trade at Champeny Brothers store. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, nor where Champeny Brothers’ store was located.

title: Scotland, South Dakota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: This round silver tag includes the engraving "Scotland, 3-17-94" on one side and "G.S. Wahlstzdt" on the other. There is no further information on when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Wedehase and Stearns Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: This round, metal Owney tag is marked with the name "J.E. Wedehase" on one side and "F. P. Stearns" on the other. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, nor to the identity of Wedehase or Stearns.

title: Scotland, South Dakota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 3/4 in. (3.18 x 1.91 cm)
descriptions: The design of this oval-shaped, metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. This one was presented by A. E. Parmenter of Dakota Valley Mills in Scotland, South Dakota. And although the tag is marked” Scotland P.O. 1883” on one side, the date March 17, 1897, reflects when it was given to Owney.

title: Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 in. (3.81 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this acorn-shaped tag from F. W. Campbell. The tag indicates that Owney is “known by number 150631.” Equitable Accidents Insurance Company of Cincinnati, Ohio, produced the tag, and Campbell is listed as a state agent for the company.

title: San Antonio, Texas Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: While in San Antonio, Texas, Owney received a coin commemorating the Alamo, the site of a famous battle between Mexico and Texas. The round metal coin centers an image of the Alamo between the phrase, “Remember the Alamo.” About one hundred eighty-nine men, including such famous figures in American history as Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie, died defending the Alamo in March 1836. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.

title: Worcester and Norwich Railway Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this round metal tag while riding a Worcester and Norwich RPO train car on October 12, 1894.

title: Manchester, New Hampshire Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1/2 in. (3.18 x 1.27 cm)
descriptions: The design of this oval-shaped, metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. This tag was given to Owney by Ralph Pearson, who listed his address on the tag as 28 Warren Street, Manchester, New Hampshire. Pearson drew a star in a circle on the back side of the tag. There is no available information to indicate when Pearson gave Owney this tag.

title: Lancaster, New Hampshire Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 3/4 x 1 in. (6.99 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: This tag was given to Owney in Lancaster, New Hampshire, on June 20, 1894. It is the first tag Owney received while visiting Lancaster. He received a second tag on a visit there two years later.

title: Tilton, New Hampshire Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 1/4 in. (3.18 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Thomas E. Fletcher gave this tag to Owney when the dog visited the small town of Tilton, New Hampshire, on May 2, 1896. Fletcher served as Tilton’s postmaster from April 7, 1894, to May 24, 1898.

title: Mitchell, South Dakota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this celebration token while visiting Mitchell, South Dakota. The front of the token displays an image of the city’s 1892 Corn Belt Exposition building of 1892. The exposition, which ran from September 28 to October 6, 1892, helped lay the foundation for the creation of the “Mitchell Corn Palace” which remains a popular tourist attraction today. The back of the tag includes a short verse titled “South Dakota’s Invitation” and reads:
TO THE WEST OF MINNESOTA
AND BEYOND FAIR IOWA TOO,
LIES THE COUNTRY SOUTH DAKOTA,
WHERE THE SKIES ARE EVER BLUE.
SO STRANGER COME AND FIND A HOME
IF FORTUNE YOU PURSUE,
TIS A GLORIOUS LAND OF PRAIRIES GRAND
AND JUST THE PLACE FOR YOU.

title: Hinton, West Virginia Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 in. (3.18 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: The small town of Hinton, West Virginia, was well known to employees of the Railway Mail Service. The Chesapeake and Ohio Railway built a line through the town in the 1870s, making it a major terminal point. The clerks who ended their day at Hinton and stayed overnight for their next assignment remember the long, tiring hike up to the railroad hotel located on a high hill above the tracks. Handmade scratches in the tag indicate that it was presented to Owney on September 13, 1894. It is marked on the back with the initials WHP and EOP, but there is no additional information indicating what these initials represent.

title: Chicago, Illinois Medallion Owney Tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
descriptions: The dog that was called Owney by U.S. mail clerks had a 9-year career (1888-1897) as a self-appointed canine guardian of the mail and postal mascot. Beginning with his appearance in the fall of 1888 at the Albany, New York, Post Office, he accompanied mail pouches being forwarded by rail throughout the United States and the world.

When his railway excursions started, the Albany mail clerks began the tradition of the "Owney tag" by fastening a note to his collar asking employees of the Railway Mail Service to record his journeys by attaching leather and metal baggage tags. As this became popular, Postmaster General John Wanamaker presented the dog with a special harness-like jacket on which to distribute the tags. In addition to the 1893 Chicago, Illinois, Swedish medal shown here, Owney was presented with more than one thousand baggage claim tags, hotel key checks, tokens, badges, coins, buttons and other trinkets.

Owney's travels, recorded by these tags and legend, took him to Canada, Mexico and Alaska. And in 1895 he traveled from Tacoma, Washington to Japan, China, Singapore, Suez, Algiers and the Azores via the steamships "Victoria" and "Port Phillip" before returning to New York City and then by rail to Tacoma. He was sent by registered mail during part of this round-the-world journey, labeled as "Registered Dog Package".
Between 1893 and 1897, Owney was presented with many special awards and medals by kennel clubs and dog shows in recognition of his nationwide celebrity.
See also the related object records in this series ("Owney tags") and the record for the Dog: Owney.

title: Boston, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received a token for a 25 cent lunch at Woodbury’s in Boston, Massachusetts, on April 27, 1892.

title: El Paso, Texas Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney’s visit to El Paso, Texas, was commemorated with this round silver tag that offered him one drink at the parlor of the city court house. The front of the tag features the image of a church, identified on the tag as the “old church age 270 years.” On the back of the tag, E.W. Ford scratched his name into it, probably to indicate that he presented the tag to Owney.

title: Chicago & Northwestern Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 3/4 in. (3.81 x 1.91 cm)
descriptions: The design of this oval-shaped, metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. This tag was given to Owney by H. P. Meise, a switchman on the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad line. The back side of the tag reads, “Returning these will suitably rewarded.” The tag is also marked with "1884," which is too early to have been the year given to Owney, but may indicate the year Meise first made the tag.

title: Columbian Exposition Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: In 1893, Chicago, Illinois, was a major US railway hub and home to one of the largest, brassiest expositions in American history – the World’s Columbian Exposition. Thousands of people, and at least one dog, visited the fair from across the US and around the world. The tag presented to Owney includes a representation of Christopher Columbus on one side and a list of names on the other: F.L. Block, V.B. Curtis, N.A. Mowr, F. Burdie, and J. Garsbard. There is no further information on these individuals or their connection to Owney.

Celebrating the 400th anniversary of Columbus’s first voyage to the new world, the Columbian Exposition was a financial and critical success that drew the attention of the world. Some of the nation’s most renowned architects, including Louis Sullivan, Frederick Law Olmsted, and Daniel Burham contributed to the exposition. One of Daniel Burham’s later projects was the City Post Office of Washington, DC, that is now home to the National Postal Museum.

title: Nashville, Tennessee Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from Post Office Department clerks working out of the Nashville, Tennessee, post office on April 9, 1892. The tag does not have specific names on it and may have been given in recognition of the approximately 60 men and women who worked as clerks in the Nashville post office during the years of Owney’s visits.

title: Baltimore, Maryland Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this uniquely decorated token from Dr. Alfred J. Brown, a Baltimore dentist. The tag notes Brown’s name, profession, location and date of the gift on one side, and the notation that it is “A canine tooth for Oney” (a misspelling of the dog’s name) on the other. Baltimore was a common stop for Owney during his travels.

title: St. Louis, Missouri Fire Department Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/2 x 3/4 in. (6.35 x 1.91 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from the St. Louis, Missouri fire department. There is no additional information from the tag to indicate when it was given to the dog. St. Louis was a large railway town, and Owney would have traveled through it many times during his travels.

title: Puyallup Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 in. (5.08 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification tag from Charles Davis of Puyallup, Washington. Davis was not a postal employee but worked for the Northern Pacific Railroad. By the 1920 census Davis had been promoted to coach foreman in that company. Puyallup was along the railway’s line into Tacoma, Washington. Both cities were popular stops for the traveling pooch.

title: Piqua Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 × 2 1/4 in. (5.72 × 5.72 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from someone promoting Ohio tin manufacturing. The token is in the shape of a tin plate, much like the ones presented to the country by William McKinley (then running for governor of Ohio) as proof that tin mining and production was possible in the United States. Rival newspapers alleged that Professor Sydney Norton of Ohio State University analyzed the tin plates and revealed that they consisted of 87 ½-percent iron, 3-percernt lead, and only 9-pecent tin. The issue was a minor bump in McKinley’s ultimately successful campaign to become Ohio’s governor. The token is the only politically-associated one that remains in the Owney tag collection.

title: Corry, Pennsylvania Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the postal employees of Corry, Pennsylvania on May 26, 1893. Corry was a busy railway town, served by the New York & Lake Erie line, the Pennsylvania and Lake Erie line, and the Western New York & Pennsylvania railway line. According to the official register of postal employees, the tag represented the town’s four postal staff members: J.B. Patterson, the town postmaster, and postal clerks Harriet O. Carlburg, James Davidson, and Walter E. Guignon.

title: H.B. Sackett Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 in. (2.54 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification tag from H. B. Sackett, who identifies himself on the back of the tag as a US mail driver for the “P.O.D.” (Post Office Department). The tag is dated 1893. Sackett lists his home on 38 North 7th Street, in Council Bluffs, Iowa. The city, on the Iowa/Nebraska border, had several railway lines running through it. Among those lines were the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy; the Chicago, Rock Island, & Pacific; the Omaha & St. Louis; and the Chicago, Milwaukee, & St. Paul.

title: William H. Waldron Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 x 1 1/4 in. (1.59 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification tag from William H. Waldron who was a distributing clerk in the Council Bluffs, Iowa post office. The reverse side of the tag has the initials “JR.O.U.A.M.,” indicating that Waldron was a junior member of the United American Mechanics, originally a nativist organization that grew out of the anti-Catholic and anti-foreign labor sentiments of the mid nineteenth century. Council Bluffs, on the Iowa/Nebraska border, had several railway lines running through it. Among those lines were the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy; the Chicago, Rock Island, & Pacific; the Omaha & St. Louis; and the Chicago, Milwaukee, & St. Paul.

title: Toledo, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/16 × 1 5/16 in. (3.33 × 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this promotional token from the Toledo, Ohio, produce exchange. The token notes that it would make Owney “our guest” on March 26, 1894. The exchange was located on the corner of Madison and St. Clair Streets in Toledo. Among the railway lines that could have brought Owney into town were the Wheeling & Lake Erie; the Columbus, Hocking Valley, & Toledo; the Lake Shore & Michigan Southern; and the Ann Arbor.

title: St. Clairsville, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from John P. Butcher, a railway mail clerk who worked the Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania to Chicago, Illinois mail train run. Butcher was appointed to his post in St. Clairsville, Belmont County, Ohio.
