title: Knights Hospitaller Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from a member of a fraternal organization known as the Knights Hospitaller. There is no additional information on when Owney received the tag.

title: Worcester, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from a druggist in Worcester, Massachusetts. Phenyo Caffein Company produced a series of metal tangle puzzles dubbed the “Chilian [sic] Puzzle” and distributed as an advertising gimmick for their headache medicine. The token Owney received was only a small part of the original puzzle, which included another token of the same size, a ring, and chain with long links. The challenge in this puzzle was to untangle and free the ring on the device and then put it back on. The Phenyo Caffein Company was owned by Julius Garst and based in Worcester, Massachusetts. Garst, originally from Ohio, worked as a physician in Worcester through the 1890s.

title: Iowa Banker's Association Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this commemorative medal while traveling in Iowa. The medal celebrates the 7th annual convention of the Iowa Bankers’ Association. One side of the medal notes the event, which took place in Council Bluffs, Iowa on May 23-24, 1893. The other side depicts scenes from around the state, including a central image of the state capitol.

title: St. Louis, Missouri Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 x 7/8 in. (2.22 x 2.22 cm)
descriptions: One token Owney received while visiting St. Louis, Missouri was from a company that is still in existence today. This token came from an employee of the Anheuser-Busch Brewing Association. The token includes the company’s symbol on one side (the Eagle and letter A had been used to identify the company since 1872), and a notice celebrating annual shipments of 20,000 train car loads of Budweiser for the year. Although the company’s products were shipped as cargo, not through the US mail, those employed by the company to move the cargo undoubtedly interacted with other workers on the train cars, including the Railway Post Office clerks (and their occasional canine visitor). The company had begun using refrigerated railway cars in the 1880s.

title: Mitchell, South Dakota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 3/4 in. (2.54 x 1.91 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from an American Express company (at this time the company’s focus was on the safe transportation of goods) employee, J.E. Wedehase, of Mitchell, South Dakota. Although they worked for separate organizations, railway mail clerks and express company employees undoubtedly knew each other and Wedehase was obviously familiar with the clerks’ canine mascot.

title: Lee Arnett Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from Lee Arnett, a leading Lincoln, Nebraska businessman during a visit to the town in 1893. Arnett had a metal manufacturing and cutting business that expanded from producing wheel scrapers to agricultural implements to corrugated metal culverts for water drainage. The token Arnett gave Owney included symbols from his membership in the Knights of Pythias, an organization dedicated to peace and friendship. Lincoln was a popular railway stop, serviced by a number of lines during Owney’s lifetime, including the Sioux City & Pacific; the Union Pacific; the Missouri Pacific; the Burlington & Missouri River; and the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific lines.

title: Aetna House hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 × 1 5/8 in. (4.13 × 4.13 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check tag from the Aetna House hotel in Danville, Illinois. The four story Aetna House was known at the time as one of the town’s finest hotels. The town was served by a number of railway lines, including the Chicago & Northwest; Mobile & Chicago; Louisville & Nashville; Chicago & Eastern Illinois; Chicago & Alton; Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul; and the Cleveland, Cincinnati, Chicago & St. Louis lines.

title: Fort Wayne, Indiana Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from an individual who noted his residence “Randolf Hotel” and city “Ft. Wayne,” but did not engrave his last name on the token which notes that Owney “stopped with Dick” in Ft. Wayne on March 27, 1894.

title: New Richmond, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 3 1/4 in. (1.91 x 8.26 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from an individual identifying himself as “L. March” of New Richmond, Ohio. The date September 12, 1894 is also engraved into the token. New Richmond was a small town accessible by rail through a side line of the Cincinnati & Eastern railroad.

title: Santa Fe, New Mexico button Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 × 5/8 in. (1.59 × 1.59 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this uniform coat button from an employee of the Santa Fe Railroad. The button was produced by the Scovill Manufacturing Company of Waterbury, Connecticut. There is no additional information to indicate when the button was given to the dog.

title: Button Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this button from an railway employee. The button was manufactured by the American Railway Supply Company of New York, New York. There is no additional information to indicate who gave the token to the dog, or when it was received. At this point the identification “USX” on the button is also unidentified.

title: Railway Mail Service button Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this button from a Railway Mail Service, Post Office Department (POD) clerk. The button was produced by the Scovill Manufacturing Company of Waterbury, Connecticut. There is no additional information to indicate when the button was given to the dog.

title: Button Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 × 5/8 in. (1.59 × 1.59 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this button manufactured by the Pettibone Manufacturing Company of Cincinnati, Ohio. The button bears a star and the word “TEXAS.” There is no additional information to indicate who gave the button to the dog or when it was received.

title: Button Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 × 5/8 in. (1.59 × 1.59 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this button while traveling on the Southern Pacific Railroad. There is no additional information to indicate who gave the button to the dog, or when it was received.

title: Button Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this uniform jacket button from a Post Office Department (POD) letter carrier. The button was produced by the Waterbury Button Company of Waterbury, Connecticut. There is no additional information to indicate who presented the button to Owney or when it was given to the dog.

title: Button Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this uniform button from an employee in the New York, New York post office. The button was produced by the Scovill Manufacturing Company of Waterbury, Connecticut. There is no additional information to indicate when the button was given to the dog.

title: Button Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this uniform button during his travels. The button was manufactured by the Waterbury Button Company of Waterbury, Connecticut. There is no additional information to indicate who gave the button to the dog, or when it was presented.

title: Charleston, West Virginia Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 x 1 5/8 in. (2.86 x 4.13 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token decoratively-framed token from Fred S. White, who worked as a post office clerk in the Charleston, West Virginia post office. White scratched his name into the back of the sterling silver token.

title: Chillicothe, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from Henry Merkle, who owned a restaurant and saloon near the Chillicothe, Ohio railroad. Owney may have traveled to Chillicothe aboard the Scioto Valley, Dayton & Ironton, or the Cincinnati, Washington & Baltimore Railroad. One of Henry Merkle’s sons, Glenmore Merkle, served as a bartender at the family saloon and later operated a liquor store and offered trade check tokens for five cents off goods.

title: Maysville, Kentucky Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Among the tokens given to Owney during his travels were dog license tags. This license shows that Owney has been legally registered in the city of Maysville, Kentucky. The name on the back side of the tag, W.H. Cae, has not yet been identified; Cae does not appear in registry of postal employees.

title: Manitou, Colorado Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the Hiawatha Club of Manitou, Colorado, a small town not far from Colorado Springs. Manitou was served by the Denver & Rio Grande Railroad.

title: Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/2 x 1 3/8 in. (6.35 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this rectangular shaped metal tag, marked Duffy, Ferris and Spence, Mounted Collectors, Cincinnati, post office, during a visit to Cincinnati, Ohio. The tag includes markings by hand of the date, September 6, 1894. The tag was created by G.G. Wright & Sons in Cincinnati.

title: Chesapeake & Ohio Railway Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/8 in. (3.81 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check token while traveling along the Chesapeake & Ohio Railway. The “local” marking indicates that the tag was meant for use on the main line, not for someone traveling onto another railway line. The tag was manufactured by Edmund Hoole’s Manufacturing Company of New York City.

title: Buffalo & Pittsburgh Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this railway baggage check token while riding on the Buffalo & Pittsburgh Railroad. The token shows that it would have been used for baggage originating in Washington, D.C. The tag was manufactured by Edmund Hoole’s Manufacturing Company of New York City.

title: New Jersey Midland Rail Yard Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check token that indicates a trip on New Jersey’s Midland Railway Company from Brooklyn, New York on an annex boat. Annex boats carried passengers, luggage, and mail between New York City, Brooklyn, and New Jersey railway stations. An annex boat for the Midland Railway landed at Jersey City, New Jersey. The token was manufactured by L.G. Tillotson & Company. Luther Gene Tillotson was an English immigrant who became an electrician and an important manufacturer of telegraph machinery in the United States. The company produced a number of other products, including railway baggage tokens.

title: Bell Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: No information is available on when or where Owney received this hollow bell and rattle.

title: Mascoutah Kennel Club Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 7/8 × 1 7/8 in. (4.76 × 4.76 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this medal engraved in his honor from Chicago’s Mascoutah Kennel Club. The club, founded in 1888, had held its first show in April 1889. The medal face features the mythological three-headed dog Cerberus, who guarded the underworld. Such an image would be quite appropriate for Owney, who was famous as a guardian of mail bags. The back of the medal is engraved “Awarded to Owney the Globe Trotter, Chicago, 1897.”

title: S.C. Kennel Club Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/16 × 1 5/16 in. (3.33 × 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this specially engraved medal when he attended the Southern California Kennel Club in April 1893. According to a report in the Los Angeles Times on April 21, 1893, Owney was a star of the show. His presence was not only noted in a headline to the story “Owney, the Mail Service Traveler, on Exhibition,” but was the leading story in the newspaper’s report on the show. “Contrary to the general rules of bench shows, Owney, the celebrated canine traveler . . . was yesterday taken in charge by the club and assigned to a stall near the entrance, where he has been a drawing card all day.” The medallion reads:
Bench Show
S.C. Kennel Club
Los Angeles, Cal.
April 1893
Special for best Traveled dog.

title: Butterfly Bench Show Association Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 13/16 × 1 13/16 in. (4.6 × 4.6 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this specially-engraved medal during an 1896 dog show in Grand Rapids, Michigan. The tag notes that it was awarded to “Owney the Globe Trotter” by the Butterfly Bench Show of Grand Rapids. On December 10, 1896, the Los Angeles Times noted that the show opened with “300 entries divided into eighty classes. The exhibits are of a much better class than last year, including some of the finest dogs in the country.” Owney’s fame as a “Globe Trotter” was in reference to the trip he made the previous fall, following mailbags around the world on ocean steamers.

title: Pacific Kennel Club Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 × 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 × 0.32 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this specially-engraved medal during his 1893 appearance at San Francisco’s Pacific Kennel Club dog show. A San Francisco Call reporter “interviewed” Owney for the paper, noting that the dog had “risen from comparative obscurity to be the best-known dog in the United States.” According to the reporter, Owney’s reply was a canine variation of the American “can do” spirit. That Owney “wishes it represents in the minds of the people that he is an example of what a dog can do for himself if he will only try.” The reverse of the medal is inscribed: "Presented to Owney by the Pacific Kennel Club / San Francisco / May 6, 1893."

title: Mitchell, South Dakota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this celebration token while visiting Mitchell, South Dakota. The front of the token displays an image of the city’s 1892 Corn Belt Exposition building of 1892. The exposition, which ran from September 28 to October 6, 1892, helped lay the foundation for the creation of the “Mitchell Corn Palace” which remains a popular tourist attraction today. The back of the tag includes a short verse titled “South Dakota’s Invitation” and reads:
TO THE WEST OF MINNESOTA
AND BEYOND FAIR IOWA TOO,
LIES THE COUNTRY SOUTH DAKOTA,
WHERE THE SKIES ARE EVER BLUE.
SO STRANGER COME AND FIND A HOME
IF FORTUNE YOU PURSUE,
TIS A GLORIOUS LAND OF PRAIRIES GRAND
AND JUST THE PLACE FOR YOU.

title: Atlanta Constitution Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/16 in. (3.81 x 2.7 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while visiting the Atlanta Constitution, a daily newspaper. Owney frequently visited newspapers in towns (after first visiting the local post office) and was a great favorite of reporters around the country. There is no information to indicate when Owney received this tag. Atlanta, Georgia was home to several railway lines that Owney traveled.

title: Portland, Oregon Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token advertising Mitchell, Lewis & Staver manufacturing company’s Portland, Oregon, office. As the token indicates, the company produced agricultural implements, including a vehicle designated the “Mitchell Wagon,” pictured on the back of the token with the nickname “the old reliable.” There is no information to indicate when the dog received this tag.

title: Laconia, New Hampshire Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 3/4 in. (3.18 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this decorative token from John O’Laughlin on May 1, 1896. At that time, O’Laughlin was a clerk at the Laconia, New Hampshire post office.

title: Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from a Cincinnati, Ohio daily newspaper, The Commercial Gazette, on April 12, 1892. Almost a dozen railway lines ran through Cincinnati during Owney’s lifetime, and the dog visited the city several times. The token was manufactured by James Murdock, Jr.’s stamp cutter company of Cincinnati, located on Longworth Avenue.

title: Milwaukee, Wisconsin Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 x 1 in. (2.86 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this dog tax license tag while in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The tag, number 694, was given to Owney in 1893. Unlike most of his more decorative gifts, a dog license tag was a practical gift for Owney, allowing him to roam the city legally.

title: Minneapolis Industrial Exposition Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this souvenir token from supporters of the Minneapolis Industrial Exposition. The exposition ran for six weeks in 1886 (two years before Owney’s journeys began) and was located in a large, six-story structure that was built at the cost of one-third of a million dollars.

title: Cheyenne, Wyoming Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 × 15/16 in. (2.38 × 2.38 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the Wyoming Tribune, a Cheyenne newspaper. It is unclear when Owney received this tag. Owney may have arrived in town by one of the railways that service Cheyenne, including the Union Pacific line or Burlington & Missouri River Railroad.

title: Yellowstone Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this room key token from the Yellowstone Hotel in Glendive, Montana Territory. Glendive is located near the eastern Montana border, between the Yellowstone River and the Badlands. The token was created at the North West Stamp Works, located at 110 East Third Street in St. Paul, Minnesota.

title: Mailing Clerks Denver, Colorado Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 2 3/16 in. (1.91 x 5.56 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the clerks in the Denver, Colorado post office on August 13, 1894. About 50 clerks worked in the post office during the days of Owney’s visits to the city. Among the railway lines that Owney may have ridden into the city were the Kansas Pacific and the Denver Pacific railroads.

title: Sidney, Nebraska Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this dog license tax token while visiting the town of Sidney, Nebraska in the south west section of the state. He probably reached the town while traveling aboard the Union Pacific railroad line.

title: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 2 in. (2.54 x 5.08 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the Chief Clerk of the Railway Mail Service office in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania on April 25, 1892. At least a half a dozen railway lines could have carried Owney into the city during his travels.

title: Davenport, Iowa Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 x 1 1/2 in. (3.49 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this aptly designed dog house license tag while visiting Davenport, Iowa in 1894. The license number, 944, is printed on the side of the dog house. The license was probably purchased for Owney by his postal worker friends, who were likely the ones to have inscribed the initials “P.O.“ (Post Office) on the back.

title: Central Railroad of New Jersey Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 15/16 x 1 3/4 in. (4.92 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check tag while passing through the Plainfield, New Jersey station on the Central Railroad of New Jersey. There is no additional information to indicate the maker of the tag or when it was given to the dog.

title: Hotel Ruhl Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 3/4 in. (5.08 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token from the Hotel Ruhl in Jackson, Michigan. The five-story Ruhl Hotel stood out among other buildings in late-nineteen-century Jackson. The hotel was owned by Charles Ruhl, a German-born immigrant, and stood not far from the Michigan Central Railroad station. Today this train station serves Amtrak passengers.

title: Columbus, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token during his travels. The item includes the initials “B.B.” and the city of Columbus, Ohio. There is no additional information to indicate if “B.B.” represented an individual or a business.

title: Central Engine Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/16 x 1 1/4 in. (2.7 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token advertising Fred A. Leonard’s Central Engine fire station. Leonard was listed as a driver for the Central Engine in the 1891 Taunton, Massachusetts, city directory. The back of the token shows a sketch of a fire engine of the period. Taunton was served by a handful of railway lines, including the New Bedford Railroad and the Old Colony & Newport Railroad.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 in. (2.86 cm)
descriptions: There is little information available to indicate where or from whom Owney received this token. One side of the token is engraved with the number 30, and the back has the letters “T” and “G” etched into the metal.

title: Bunkerhill Car House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 5/16 in. (1.91 x 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Robert R. Waugh. The token identifies the Bunker Hill Car House in Boston, Massachusetts. The car house belonged to the West End Street Railroad company, which operated a mail streetcar in Boston. There is no information to indicate when Owney received the token, he visited Boston so often that the city’s postal workers considered him to belong to them almost as much as he belonged to the Albany post office. In some areas, city’s mail streetcars were manned with clerks re-assigned from Railway Mail Service train cars.

title: Helena, Montana Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 5/16 in. (3.81 x 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check token while in Helena, Montana. There is no additional information to indicate when Owney was in the city, or when he received the token.

title: Seattle, Washington Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 in. (3.81 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this advertising token from watchmakers Simon Rumpf and Joseph Mayer. There is no additional information to indicate when Owney received the token, but by 1894 Simon Rumpf had fled the area, and possibly the country, while under investigation for fraud. By the next year, Joseph Mayer had started up a new jewelry wholesale business, Joseph Mayer and Bros., with his brothers Albert and Markus. Either Owney was given an old token, or he received it before Simon Rumpf and Joseph Mayer’s business was dissolved in 1894.

title: St. James Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 1 3/4 in. (5.72 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel room key token from the St. James Hotel of Corry, Pennsylvania. There is no additional information to indicate when he received the token. A number of railroads passed through Corry during Owney’s lifetime. He may have arrived in town on the Philadelphia & Erie; the Lake Erie & Western; or the New York & Erie Railroad.

title: Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 × 1 3/4 in. (4.45 × 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this railway baggage check token while visiting the Washington, DC depot of the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad. The depot was located at Pennsylvania Avenue and 2nd Street, NW, an area now used for parking. Owney visited the nation’s capital on a number of occasions; there is nothing on this token to indicate when it was given to the traveling canine.

title: Canadian Pacific Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 3/4 in. (4.45 x 1.91 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check token while traveling on the Canadian Pacific Railroad. There is no additional information to indicate when the token was given to the dog.

title: Illinois Central Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this baggage check token in Jackson, Mississippi while traveling on the Illinois Central Railroad. There is no additional information to indicate who gave the token to Owney.

title: Saulpaugh Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 3/4 in. (5.08 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel key check token while visiting the Saulpaugh Hotel (also called the Grand Saulpaugh Hotel) in Mankato, Minnesota. There is no indication on the tag when Owney visited the large, four-story luxury hotel, or how he arrived in town. Mankato hosted a number of railway lines, including the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul; the Chicago & Northwestern; and the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis & Omaha.

title: Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 9/16 in. (3.18 x 3.97 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the Cincinnati, Ohio postal workers. There is no information on the token to indicate when he received the tag. Cincinnati was a well-connected spot for America’s railroads in the late nineteenth century and Owney visited the city on several occasions. The tag, from the city’s “post office clerks” represented the approximately 250 men and women who worked as clerks in that office in the 1890s.

title: Phoenix Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 5/16 in. (3.81 x 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel room key token from the Phoenix Hotel in Corry, Pennsylvania. There is no additional information on the tag to indicate when it was given to Owney. The town of Corry was served by a number of railway lines, and Owney traveled into and through Corry on a number of occasions.

title: Ogden House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 x 1 5/16 in. (2.86 x 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel room key token from the Ogden Hotel of Council Bluffs, Iowa. The original Ogden Hotel had burned down in 1874 and was rebuilt a few years later. Like its predecessor, the second Ogden Hotel was considered the finest in the area for many years. No information is on the tag to indicate when it was presented to Owney, who visited that town at least three different times.

title: Binghamton, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Cleveland Robinson, a clerk at the Binghamton, New York, post office in the 1890s. A number of railway lines traveled through Binghamton, including the New York & Western Railroad.

title: Westminster and Vancouver Tramway Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/4 in. (3.81 x 4.45 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token on one of his visits into Canada. While visiting Vancouver, British Columbia, he may have ridden on the Westminster and Vancouver Tramway, which opened in October 1891. The tramway was the continent’s first inter-urban electric railway, carrying passengers (and possibly a traveling dog), but no mail, between New Westminster and downtown Vancouver. There is no indication of when Owney received this tag, or what the number, 0004 stood for.

title: Butler Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 15/16 x 1 15/16 in. (4.92 x 4.92 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this rather plain looking hotel room key token while visiting the large and luxurious Butler Hotel in Seattle, Washington. The five-story hotel was located at 2nd and James Streets. Owney visited Seattle and the nearby town of Tacoma, Washington on a regular basis. There is no additional information on this tag to indicate when it was given to the dog.

title: Willaim F. Maybaum Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width (with "key ring"): 1 3/4 x 1 1/8 in. (4.45 x 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from William F. Maybaum, a Brooklyn, New York, postal clerk. Maybaum worked in the main, or general, post office (“G.P.O.”) in Brooklyn. There is no additional information on when the tag was given to the dog. Maubaum is listed as a worker in the Brooklyn post office through the 1890s.

title: Mitchell, South Dakota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/8 in. (3.81 x 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this practical gift from someone in Mitchell, South Dakota. The dog license tag shows that someone has covered Owney’s dog tax, giving the dog a form of legal status within the city. There is no additional information to indicate who gave this tag to Owney.

title: Humane Burial Association Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 9/16 × 1 9/16 in. (3.97 × 3.97 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the Humane Burrial [sic] Association, Incorporated during his travels. There is no additional information to indicate when he received the token, or who gave it to the dog.

title: Good for 5 cent Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
descriptions: There is little information to indicate where and when Owney received this trade check token. The token is marked good for five cents “in trade” on the front. The back of the token has the name Holtrup.

title: Omaha, Nebraska Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from John P. O’Connor of Omaha, Nebraska. O’Connor was a mail distribution clerk at the Omaha post office. There is no indication of when he presented this token to Owney. His identification token lists his address as the Millard Hotel, a large five-story hotel that was owned and operated as part of the Pacific Hotel Company, which operated hotels along the Union Pacific railroad line. Owney is known to have been in the city in 1893 and 1894. Remarking on one of Owney’s visits, the ‘Omaha Daily Bee’ newspaper noted that he “arrived in the city from the east, and after spending the day visiting points of interest about [nearby] Council Bluffs left for the west by the Overland flyer.”
Reference:
‘Omaha Daily Bee’, Sunday, March 25, 1894.

title: Bell Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 7/8 x 7/8 x 7/8 in. (2.22 x 2.22 x 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this little bell during his travels. There is no information to indicate when or where it was given to the dog.

title: Lowell, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 x 1 1/4 in. (1.59 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Thomas L. Dickey of Lowell, Massachusetts. There is no indication on when Owney received the tag. Dickey worked in the insurance business, specializing as the tag notes, in fire insurance. Lowell was an active railway town in the late 1890s, with at least five different lines running in and out of the town for Owney to choose from.

title: Key-shape Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1/2 in. (5.08 x 1.27 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this key from J.R. Sutton. There is no additional information to indicate Sutton’s relationship with Owney or the Post Office Department or when he presented the key to the dog.

title: Key-shape Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1/2 in. (3.18 x 1.27 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this key during his travels. There is no information on the item to indicate who gave it to Owney, or when the dog received the key.

title: Athens, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 1/2 in. (2.54 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while visiting Athens, Ohio on September 17, 1894. From Owney’s tag collection, we know that he visited Logan, Ohio the very next day (object number 0.052985.414). For that trip, Owney would have probably ridden on the Columbus, Hocking Valley & Toledo Railroad line. Athens was also serviced by the Toledo & Ohio Central and the Baltimore & Ohio Southwestern railroads and Owney could have arrived in town on either.

title: International Order of King's Daughters and Sons Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 3/4 in. (1.91 x 1.91 cm) Height x Width (with d-ring): 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token during his travels. The item indicates it was given to Owney by a member of the International Order of King’s Daughters and Sons (IHN stands for “In His Name”). There is no additional information to indicate who owned the tag or when it was given to the dog.

title: New York, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/16 × 1 1/16 in. (2.7 × 2.7 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token during his travels. The token is identified as from “Com.Tel.Co.” and a “Fire Alarm” token. The token may have been from the Commercial Telegraph Company of New York City, New York. There is no additional information to indicate when Owney received the tag, or who gave it to the dog.

title: Renova, Pennsylvania Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 in. (4.45 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the Smyth Brothers’ Jewelry store in Renova, Pennsylvania. The store was owned and operated by John and James Smyth, working as jewelers and opticians. Owney may have arrived in town on the Philadelphia & Erie Railroad. There is no additional information on the tag to indicate when it was given to the dog.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 in. (3.18 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: There is no additional information on this tag to indicate when or where it was given to Owney. The tag is dated 1887, which is a year before Owney began his adventures, and was probably a spare token that an individual had to spare.

title: Springfield, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Daniel C. White of Springfield, Massachusetts. White was employed as a railway worker in Springfield. There is no additional information to indicate when he presented the token to Owney.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: There is no additional information on this item to indicate when, where, or from whom Owney received the tag. The tag is marked simply with the number 25.

title: Good for 5 cents Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token from F. Schermer, a businessman whose token offered Owney 5-cents off “at the bar.” There is no additional information to indicate where Schermer lived, or when he presented the token to the dog.

title: Logan, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: 1 in Diam.
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token from a bar in Logan, Ohio. The bar was operated by John Slisher. The trade check was good for five cents at the bar. Slisher prospered in his business and continued to offer trade tokens to his customers for at least another decade.

title: Knights of Pythias Owney tag
dimensions: 1 1/8 in Diam.
descriptions: Owney received this token from an unidentified individual in Jaxon [Jackson?], Mississippi. The design at the top of the token reveals that donor was a member of the Knights of Pythias. There is no additional information available to indicate when, or from whom, Owney received the token.

title: McCabe House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 × 1 3/16 in. (3.02 × 3.02 cm)
descriptions: Owney may have received this tag from Barney McCabe, the proprietor of the McCabe House of Nashville, Tennessee. The hotel room key token has the city name, Nashville, etched on the back of the coin. The McCabe House hotel and saloon was located on 208 Walnut, across the street from the city’s Union Depot railway station. The business was doing well enough that Mr. McCabe could purchase advertisements for his establishment in directories and newspapers. McCabe had immigrated to the US from Ireland in 1852. He began work as a liquor dealer and expanded his property to include a hotel.

title: Seattle, Washington Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/16 in. (3.81 x 2.7 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this shield-shaped identification token from Victor E. Twedell of Seattle, Washington. Twedell spent time in the late 1880s and early 1890s as a waiter in Seattle restaurants. He does not seem to have any connection to the Post Office Department and may have left Seattle in the mid 1890s for California. There is no additional information on the identification token to indicate how he met Owney, or when he gave the tag to the dog.

title: Haverhill, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/4 in. (1.91 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from William J. Howe, a clerk in the Haverhill, Massachusetts post office. There is no additional information to indicate when Howe presented the tag to the dog. It may have been when Owney was in Haverhill on June 16, 1894, where he received an additional tag with that date from a separate individual. The city of Haverhill was served by at least two railway lines that could have delivered Owney into the town.

title: Samuel N. West Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 1/8 in. (2.54 x 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Samuel N. West, a Railway Mail Service (RMS) clerk who worked on railway mail trains between St. Paul, Minnesota, and Watertown, South Dakota. West is one of the few Railway Mail Service clerks whose tags are currently among Owney’s trinkets. The RMS clerks were the postal workers who allowed Owney to ride along in the cars while they were doing their work.

The top portion of the identification tag indicates that West was a member of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows (IOOF). The chain emblem with the letters “FLT” in the links stands for “Friendship, Love, and Truth.” The back side of the tag is the design of an eye (the All Seeing Eye), also a symbol used by Odd Fellows.

title: Boston, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 1/16 in. (3.18 x 2.7 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this business identification token from the Boston Safe Deposit and Trust Company of Boston, Massachusetts. The company, which is still in business today, offered a $1.00 reward for the return of any item to which the tag would have been attached. Owney made several trips to Boston and the city’s postal workers often gave him the run of the city during his visits.

title: James W. Hazen Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 in. (3.18 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from James W. Hazen of Baraboo, Wisconsin. Hazen worked briefly as a railway conductor on the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad. The symbol of a compass and square at the bottom of the token indicates that Hazen was a Freemason. There is no additional information to indicate when Hazen gave it to the dog.

title: District of Columbia Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 x 1 3/16 in. (3.02 x 3.02 cm)
descriptions: Owney was given this District of Columbia dog license tag in 1890. The license allowed Owney to legally travel along the streets of the nation’s capital. The dog license is number “1821.” There is nothing with the tag to indicate who purchased it for the dog to wear.

title: South Bend, Indiana Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/16 x 3/4 in. (3.33 x 1.91 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Orville S. Cullar, a Railway Mail Service (RMS) clerk. Cullar, born in Indiana, worked on the mail trains between New York, New York and Chicago, Illinois. While not riding the trains, Cullar lived at 1129 S. Lafayette in South Bend, Indiana.

Cullen is one of the few Railway Mail Service clerks whose tags are currently among Owney’s trinkets. The RMS clerks were the postal workers who allowed Owney to ride along in the cars while they were doing their work.

title: Boston Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 x 1 in. (3.02 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from an Irish immigrant, Michael Falvey. Falvey was working as a city letter carrier in Boston, Massachusetts. There is no additional information to indicate when Falvey gave this token to Owney.

title: Kansas City, Missouri Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 12 13/16 x 1 5/8 in. (32.6 x 4.13 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this business advertising token from Henry J. Bruner, a German immigrant who opened a hardware company in Kansas City, Missouri. The token bears the date “March 23, 1894.”

title: Waterbury, Connecticut Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 × 15/16 in. (2.38 × 2.38 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the Homes, Booth, and Haydens Company of Waterbury, Connecticut. The company, founded in 1853, was a partnership between Hiram W. Hayden, Israel Holmes, Henry H. and James A. Hayden. The company specialized in copper and brass work, including lamp manufacturing and wire for electrical use. It is not known when someone from that company presented this token to Owney.

title: Martinsburg, West Virginia Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 7/8 x 7/8 in. (4.76 x 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney receive this advertising token from John J. Homrich, a watch salesman who opened a jewelry store in Martinsburg, West Virginia in 1892. His store was near a station for the Chesapeake & Ohio Railway line.

title: Brooklyn, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 9/16 × 1 9/16 in. (3.97 × 3.97 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Thomas A. Owens, a clerk in the Brooklyn, New York post office. Owney visited a number of the New York City and Brooklyn post offices during his lifetime. There is no additional information to indicate when Owens presented Owney with this tag.

title: St. Louis, Missouri Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this advertising and personal identification token during his travels. The token was produced by the Cod-Liver Oil Glycerin Company of St. Louis, Missouri. The token advertised a new method of delivering cod liver as a medicine. The “Aluminum Pocket Piece” as it is identified on the back of the token, was given to physicians to advertise the new product. A space on the back of the token was left open for physicians to place their name and address. There is no information to indicate who gave the token to Owney or when it was given to the dog.

title: Taunton, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this heart-shaped identification token from Edmund F. Flynn, a postal clerk in Taunton, Massachusetts. There is no additional information to indicate when Owney received the tag.

title: Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 in. (2.54 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this dog tax license token while visiting Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada. According to stories in some US newspapers, Owney was once detained in Canada for not having a valid dog license. Perhaps his postal clerk friends purchased this token for him in 1895 in the hopes he would have a trouble-free visit in Winnipeg.

title: Minneapolis, Minnesota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/16 x 1 in. (3.33 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this advertising token from Moses L. Cohen, a pawnbroker and jewelry dealer in Minneapolis, Minnesota. As noted on the pocket-watch-shaped token, Cohen’s business was located at 6 Washington Avenue, North, and was established in 1879. Minneapolis was a bustling railway town during Owney’s lifetime. He visited the city a few times. Among the train lines that accessed the city were the St. Paul & Duluth, Minneapolis; the St. Paul & Sault Ste. Marie; the Great Northern, Minneapolis & St. Louis; and the Northern Pacific railways.

title: Corry, Pennsylvania Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this key ring and business identification token from the Pennsylvania Mutual Accident Society, a Pennsylvania life insurance business. Unlike Owney’s other tokens, this one opens up for a compartment that could hold additional information. This tag was owned by L.F. Tumble of Corry, Pennsylvania, whose name is written on the inside of the tag, along with the number 93, indicating the year (1893) that Tumble presented this token to Owney.

This tag style was patented as noted on the tag on January 27, 1895. The patent was held by Frederick H. Laforge and J. Richard Smith of Watertown, Connecticut. Laforge and Smith were both officers in the Connecticut Mutual Steam Boiler Inspection and Insurance Company. In later years Smith manufactured metal novelties and Laforge continued work as a boiler inspector.

title: Brooklyn, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 x 2 5/16 in. (1.59 x 5.87 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this dog license tag while visiting Brooklyn, New York in 1891. The tag provided for Owney to legally be on the streets of the city. There is no information on who purchased the tag for the dog.

title: Los Angeles Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/16 x 3/4 in. (2.7 x 1.91 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from Frank L. Thacker, a Los Angeles, California, gunsmith and firearms dealer. The tag includes the date 1893. Owney is known to have visited Los Angeles in April 1893 when he attended a dog show in the city. There is no additional information that identifies the initials “JA” and number “13” on the other side of the tag.

title: Elroy, Wisconsin Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 x 1 1/8 in. (2.86 x 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Edgar S. Willey, a rural letter carrier in Elroy, Wisconsin. There is no information to indicate when Willey presented the token to Owney. Elroy was a stop along the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad. Symbols on top of the token indicate that Willey was a Freemason.

title: Paso Robles Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token from the Paso Robles Hotel in Paso Robles, California. The back side of the token notes that it was: “good for one drink.” There is no additional information available to indicate when the token was given to the dog. Trade checks were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

Paso Robles, located in San Luis Obispo County, California, was along a branch of the Atlantic and Pacific Railroad. The luxurious, three-story hotel opened in 1891. It included a beauty parlor, barber shop, library and billiard rooms. Guests could also enjoy the hotel’s large garden and golf course.

title: Baltimore, Maryland Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 5/16 in. (1.91 x 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from George Bevans of Baltimore, Maryland. The tag includes the date 1892 on the front side, and “American Office” on the reverse. There is no additional information to indicate when Bevans presented this token to Owney or what his relationship may have been to the Post Office Department.

title: Frank Theis Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token from Frank Theis’s saloon. The token offers 5-cents off “at the bar” to the recipient. There is no additional information to indicate where Theis’ saloon was located, or when he gave the token to Owney. Trade checks such as this were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

title: McWhorter's Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token from an establishment called McWhorter’s. The token notes that McWhorter’s was located at “221 4th Ave.,” but there is no additional information to indicate in which town it was located. The token was “good for one drink” or “10 cents” to the recipient. Trade checks such as this were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag during his travels. There is no information beyond the initials “R.B.” on the tag to indicate who may have given the tag to the dog.

title: Ontario, Canada Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 x 1 in. (3.02 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from R. L. Elliott. The token is marked Ballantrae, Ontario on one side and 489 Main Street, Winnipeg, Barber, on the other. Ballantrae is a small Canadian town that was located on a line of the Toronto and Nipissing Railway.

title: Blanchester, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token from Wilson & Swing’s Billiard Hall in Blanchester, Ohio. The token was good for “5-cents at the bar.” There is no indication on the tag when it was given to the dog. Owney may have traveled to the town on the Baltimore & Ohio Southwest railroad, or the Cincinnati, Washington, and Baltimore Railroad.

title: Camp Douglas, Wisconsin Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 3/16 x 1 1/8 in. (5.56 x 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this dog license tag while visiting Camp Douglas, Wisconsin. Camp Douglas was a small, but busy town along the railways between Milwaukee, Wisconsin and Minneapolis/St. Paul, Minnesota and where east and west trains intersected with the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad. There is no information on who purchased the license for Owney, or when it was given to the dog.

title: Bald Knob, Arkansas Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 × 15/16 in. (2.38 × 2.38 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Lawrence J. Dumas of Bald Knob, Arkansas. Dumas had a small drug store in the city. Bald Knob was located on the St. Louis Iron Mountain & Southern railway line. There is no additional information on when Dumas gave this token to Owney.

title: Binghamton, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/16 x 3/4 in. (3.33 x 1.91 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Albert H. Surdam, a letter carrier from Binghamton, New York. The tag notes that Surdam lived on Rutherford Street in Binghamton, but there is no additional information to indicate when he presented the tag to Owney.

title: Edward P. Thorn Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1/2 x 2 1/4 in. (1.27 x 5.72 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Edward P. Thorn, a saloon keeper, wines and liquors dealer from Plainfield, New Jersey. Symbols on the token indicate Thorn was a Freemasons Lodge Master. Plainfield was a stop along the Central Railroad of New Jersey.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 × 1 3/16 in. (3.02 × 3.02 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while traveling in the West. The name Sumas could indicate a hotel or business in the Dakota Territory, or the town of Sumas, Washington, along the Canadian border. There is no additional information to indicate exactly where Owney was when he received this token.

title: Los Angeles, California Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 7/16 × 1 7/16 in. (3.65 × 3.65 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from David L. Burke of Los Angeles, California. Burke owned a plumbing business. It is not known when or why he presented this token to the dog. Owney visited the city of Los Angeles several times, including once in 1893 when he was the star of a dog show in the city.

title: Pontiac, Illinois Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 7/8 in. (4.45 x 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this watch fob token from the Caldwell & McGregor jewelry store in Pontiac, Illinois. Although there is no information to indicate when the token was presented to the dog, James Caldwell retired and dissolved the partnership in 1895. Pontiac was easily reached by numerous railways, including the Wabash, the Chicago & Alton; and the Illinois Central railway lines.

title: Plymouth, New Hampshire Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 x 2 7/16 in. (1.59 x 6.19 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from William G. Hull, who served as the postmaster of Plymouth, New Hampshire from 1895-1899. Prior to his service as postmaster of Plymouth, Hull had served as the first postmaster of Livingston, New Hampshire in 1881. Hull dated this tag as “M. 5. 96.” The town of Plymouth was reached by the Boston, Concord, Montreal & White Mountains railroad as well as the Pemigewasset Valley Railroad during Owney’s lifetime.

title: Madison, Wisconsin Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Charles G. Snow of Madison, Wisconsin. There is no information to indicate when Snow gave this token to the dog. Snow held several jobs. During the years Owney was traveling, Snow worked for the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad. From 1890-18 he was an assistant night clerk for the railroad. From 1894-1895, he was a freight clerk for the company.

title: Kansas City Post Office Department Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 5/8 in. (4.45 x 4.13 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from postal clerks in Kansas City, Missouri. The item is dated March 23, 1894, one of many trips Owney made through the area. This token was produced by the Henry J. Brunner’s Hardware Company of Kansas City. The company began as a repair shop and grew into a metal and machinist supply company.

Kansas City was a major railway hub and Owney would have traveled through the town on many occasions. Among the train lines that passed through during his lifetime were the Kansas City, Osceola, & Southern Railway; the Atchison, Topeka & the Santa Fe; the Chicago, Milwaukee, & St. Paul; and the Kansas City, Pittsburgh, & Gulf railroads.

title: Chicago, Illinois Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this advertising token from Dallemand & Co., a wholesale liquor supply company based in Chicago, Illinois. The company was operated by Albert Dallemand. There is no indication from the token when it was given to Owney.

title: Taunton Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 13/16 x 1 13/16 in. (2.06 x 4.6 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag from members of the Taunton, Massachusetts post office. The Taunton post office provided their own, phonetic, spelling of Owney’s name, engraving the tag to “Onee” and presenting it to the dog on June 9, 1894. Taunton was an active railroad town, with a number of lines passing through.

title: W.C. Munsey & Co. Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token during his travels. The token indicates that it is good for 10-cents off at “W.C. Munsey & Co.” on one side, and includes the name “Palace” and “Barber Shop & Bath House” on the other. San Francisco, California had a large and famous hotel known as the “Palace,” but at this time there is no known connection between that hotel and “W.C. Munsey & Co.”

title: Cheyenne, Wyoming Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1/2 × 1/2 in. (1.27 × 1.27 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this medal from the postal workers of the Cheyenne, Wyoming post office on April 12, 1893. At that time, that office had a postmaster, three clerks, and six city letter carriers. The reverse side of the medal advertises the city of “Fair” Gallatin, Montana, nicknamed the “Egypt of America” by promoters for its fertile and productive soil. The medal may have been handy when Owney was visiting Cheyenne’s postal workers, who scratched and engraved their message into one side of the medal. The city of Gallatin is just over Wyoming’s northern border, while Cheyenne is in the far south-eastern corner.

title: San Francisco, California Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 x 7/8 in. (5.4 x 2.22 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this advertising and identification token from the Home Benefit Life Association of San Francisco, California. The token includes the embossed image of a building on one side and the “reward return to” identification on the other. There is nothing on the tag to indicate when it was given to Owney. The association was established by Frank Colton in the early 1880s and went out of business in 1892. Owney made several trips to San Francisco during his lifetime.

title: Mitchell Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 x 15 3/16 in. (2.38 x 38.52 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while visiting the town of Mitchell, South Dakota. As the tag notes, in 1889, Mitchell was still part of the Dakota Territory (the territory became North and South Dakota late in the year, on November 2, 1889). The Maltese-Cross-shaped tag includes the number 228. There is no additional information to indicate the purpose of the token.

title: Waverly, Iowa Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/16 x 1 5/16 in. (2.7 x 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from Grant E. Hirleman in Waverly, Iowa. There is no additional information on the tag to indicate Hirleman’s connection to Owney or when he presented the token to the dog. Hirleman was not a postal employee in Iowa during the 1890s.

title: Bloomington Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this item during his travels. The lettering is badly faded, with little more than the individual’s first name “James” and the town of “Bloomington” [Indiana] still visible. There is no additional information on the full identity of the donor. The item was most likely a Civil War-era soldier’s identification tag. Such tags were purchased by soldiers who wanted to insure their bodies could be identified in case of death. There is nothing with this item to indicate when it was given to Owney.

title: St. Louis, Missouri Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 × 1 3/16 in. (3.02 × 3.02 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this advertising and personal identification token during his travels. The token was produced by the Cod-Liver Oil Glycerin Company of St. Louis, Missouri. The token advertised a new method of delivering cod liver as a medicine. The “Aluminum Pocket Piece” as it is identified on the back of the token, was given to physicians to advertise the new product. A space on the back of the token was left open for physicians to place their name and address. There is no information to indicate who gave the token to Owney or when it was given to the dog.

title: Portland, Oregon Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from a group of Railway Mail Service (RMS) clerks working out of Portland, Oregon on a “South Bound” railway mail car. The token was originally produced by Mitchell Lewis & Staver Co., a Pacific Northwest machinery company that began in 1882 and is still in operation. The RMS clerks scratched out one face of the token and crudely engraved their identification information as well as the date, April 16, 1893, over that side of the coin.

title: St. Peter, Minnesota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/16 × 1 5/16 in. (3.33 × 3.33 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from W.F. Coffin of St. Peter, Minnesota. The individual who presented this tag to Owney may have been Wilbur F. Coffin, a postal clerk. The token was probably created on the engraved date of 1880, at least eight years before Owney began making his journeys. It is not known when Owney was in St. Peter, but he probably arrived in town on the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad.

title: Lawrence House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel room key token from the Lawrence House in Jackson, Mississippi. There is no additional information to indicate when the token was presented to the dog. Owney may have arrived in Jackson aboard the Illinois Central or the Yazoo & Mississippi Valley railroad.

title: Ranier Hotel Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 x 1 9/16 in. (2.38 x 3.97 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel room key token from the Rainier Hotel in Seattle, Washington. Owney made several visits to Seattle and its nearby neighbor Tacoma, Washington during his lifetime. The hotel was located between 5th and 6th avenues and between Marion and Columbia streets.

title: Pennsylvania and Erie Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 x 1 1/2 in. (2.38 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this railway baggage check token while traveling on the Pennsylvania and Erie Railroad. There is no additional information to indicate when the token was presented to the dog. The token was made by the Hoole Manufacturing Company of New York, owned and operated by Edmund Hoole.

title: Plumb House Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 1 1/2 in. (4.13 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this hotel room key token from the Plumb House hotel in Streator, Illinois. There is no additional information on when the token was given to the dog. Plumb House, located on the northwest corner of Main and Bloomington, was named for Ralph Plumb, the town’s first mayor (1882-1885). In its early days, Streator was a coal town, and grew quickly as railway lines were built to carry out the coal. Several railway lines ran through the town during Owney’s lifetime, including the Chicago, Burlington, & Quincy; the Louisville, Evansville, & St. Louis Consolidated; the Chicago & Alton; and the Peoria, Decatur, & Evansville lines.

title: Houston, Texas Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
descriptions: This is one of two tokens Owney received from Alphonse Stude’s Houston, Texas, bakery. Stude, a prominent Houston businessman and city booster, recognized the advertising potential of the traveling dog. Owney’s visits were often written up in local newspapers, with reporters often listing the tokens the dog was wearing at the time. This token, which could be used in trade for a small loaf of bread, is known as a trade check. Such tokens were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

title: Chicago, Santa Fe, and California Railroad Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 × 1 3/16 in. (3.02 × 3.02 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this railway bag check token while traveling on a local line of the Chicago, Santa Fe, and California Railroad. There is no additional information to indicate when or where the token was given to the dog. Like several other tokens presented to the dog, it was created by William W. Wilcox’s manufacturing company of Chicago, Illinois.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 x 1 1/8 in. (2.86 x 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this tag during his travels. One side of the tag includes the notation “1H” and the date “1893.” The other side has faintly legible scratches of names, “Jas Stone” and “Guy D. May” or “Guy D. Way.” There is no additional information to indicate the men’s connection to Owney or the post office.

title: Cincinnati Post Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while visiting Cincinnati, Ohio. The item may have been given to the dog by a representative of the ‘Cincinnati Post’ newspaper. There are no additional notations on the token to indicate its original function or when it was given to the dog. Owney could have arrived in town on a number of different railroads. Cincinnati grew from a bustling port city along the Ohio River into an active railroad town, with at least seven different rail lines leading into the city.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 x 1 1/2 x 1/2 in. (2.54 x 3.81 x 1.27 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token during his travels. The only information available on the item are the initials “N.U.H.” and the number 9. There is nothing to indicate when or where the token originated or who gave it to Owney.

title: San Antonio, Texas Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from members of his greatest fan club--Railway Mail Service workers. These clerks worked out of the San Antonio, Texas post office. The token is dated April 4, 1892. Owney is known to have visited San Antonio at least twice, in 1892 and in 1895.

title: Rock Island, Illinois Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 × 1 3/16 in. (3.02 × 3.02 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from John Koch, a Rock Island, Illinois gunsmith. The token includes Koch’s occupation on one side, along with the date May 9, 1895. Among the trains that Owney may have ridden on into the city were the Chicago, Rock Island, & Pacific; the Chicago & Alton; and the Chicago, Burlington, & Quincy railroads.

title: Sanborn, Iowa Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (1.27 × 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from Chauncey F. Owen, the postmaster of Sanborn, Iowa. Owen served as the town’s postmaster twice, from December 1884 to July 1885 and from February 1890 to January 1896. It would have been during his second term as Sanborn’s postmaster that he presented this token to Owney. During Owney’s lifetime, Sanborn was serviced by the Chicago, Milwaukee, & St. Paul railroad line.

title: Mitchell, South Dakota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this dog license tag during a visit to Mitchell, South Dakota. The tag shows that someone has covered Owney’s dog tax, giving him legal permission to be on the city streets, at least during the year of 1890. The tag was manufactured by S.D. Childs & Company, a Chicago, Illinois stationery and engraving firm.

title: Cedar Rapids, Iowa Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 x 1 1/4 in. (1.59 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from someone in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The token has the phrase, “Love, Purity, Fidelity” on one side, which indicates it came from someone who was a member of the Freemasons. There is no additional information on the token to indicate when it was given to the dog and at the time, no postal workers from the Cedar Rapids post office were named Horace.

title: P.J. Butler Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 × 15/16 in. (2.38 × 2.38 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this trade check token from P.J. Butler, possibly of Indianapolis, Indiana, but no additional information is available on the token to make certain identification. There is no information on the token to indicate when it was given to the dog.

title: Sioux City Corn Palace Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 15/16 in. (4.13 x 2.38 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token advertising the Corn Palace in Sioux City, Iowa. This was the last of corn palaces built in that city from 1887-1891. The 1891 Corn Palace featured a 200-foot tower with a balcony. There is no information indicating who presented this token to Owney.

title: Pierre, South Dakota Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 15/16 in. (4.13 x 2.38 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token from the employees of the Pierre, South Dakota post office. At the time of Owney’s travels there were only three people employed at that post office. Robert N. Locke was the town’s postmaster and John H. McCord, originally of Illinois, and Fred S. Williams, born in Canada, served as the town’s postal clerks.

title: Lawrence, Massachusetts Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 x 1 1/2 in. (5.4 x 3.81 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this advertising token from George Ketchum, a pharmacist who partnered with H.M. Witney in Lawrence, Massachusetts. The store was named for Whitney and located on 297 Essex Street. Ketchum had the token engraved especially for the dog, “Presented to Owney” and included the presentation date of April 25, 1896 at the bottom of the token.

title: Jackson, Mississippi Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this identification token from W. M. Bettersworth of Jackson, Mississippi. The token is dated1895. The token’s design shows that Bettersworth was a member of the Knights of Pythius, the “FCB” in the design standing for “friendship, charity, and benevolence.” There is no information with the token to indicate Bettersworth relationship with the Post Office Department, if any.

title: Hillsboro, Ohio Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 in. (3.81 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this advertising token in the shape of a pocket watch from F. Emmerling, a jeweler living in Hillsboro, Ohio. There is no information on when Emmerling gave the token to the dog. The back side carries the advertisements for “Jas. Boss” “Keystone Watch Cases.” Watch cases were sold separately from the pocket watch. Boss Keystone cases were among the most popular watch cases. The advertisement notes that Emmerling carried this cases, including the new “non-pull-out-bow” a fastener that had been patented by Keystone Watch Case Company employee Edward Chappatte in 1891.

title: Bozeman, Montana Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/8 in. (3.81 x 2.86 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this dog license tag while visiting Bozeman, Montana in 1892. There is no additional information to indicate who presented it to the dog. The tag was manufactured by E.R. Williamson of Minneapolis, Minnesota.

title: Omaha & OGD Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 1 9/16 in. (4.13 x 3.97 cm)
descriptions: Owney received this token while traveling on board the Omaha & Ogden railway mail route. The token is dated April 22, but no year is indicated. The token was given to Owney by the clerks working on the eastbound train car, Michael P. Burke, an Irish immigrant, Joseph F. Finch of Illinois, Lawrence J.A. Holst, a German immigrant, Warren J. Nash of Maine, Lawrence R. Rossiter of Ohio, Frederick R. Stuart and George G. Whitmore, both born in Nebraska.

title: Grand Rapids, Michigan Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 1 1/4 in. (5.72 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. The plate was given to the dog while he was visiting Grand Rapids, Michigan in September 1896. It notes that for Owney, at least, there was such a thing as a “free lunch,” at least in Grand Rapids. That year Owney also received a specially-engraved medal from the Butterfly Bench Show of Grand Rapids (object number 0.52985.336).

title: Milwaukee, Wisconsin Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 1/4 in. (5.08 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. He received it while in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on February 27, 1896. While the tag encourages Owney to “call again,” there is no additional information to indicate who attached this tag to the dog’s collar. Several railway lines ran through Milwaukee, connecting it with Chicago to the south and Minneapolis to the west, including the Chicago, Milwaukee, & St. Paul Railroad.

title: Rock Island, Illinois Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 5/8 x 1 3/16 in. (6.67 x 3.02 cm)
descriptions: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. He received it from the Rock Island, Illinois railway postal clerks while visiting the city in 1895.

title: Albany, New York Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 7/8 x 1 1/4 in. (7.3 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. The scalloped-edged plate bearing his name was attached to his collar by the workers at the Albany, New York post office. Owney began his travels from Albany and that city’s postal workers considered him to be part of their postal family. There is no information to indicate when this plate was attached to Owney’s collar.

title: Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 1 in. (5.72 x 2.54 cm)
descriptions: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. He received it while visiting Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania in 1892. The tag includes the number “166.” There is no definitive information available at this time to indicate the purpose of the tag, or who gave it to the dog. Numerous railway lines passed through Pittsburgh during Owney’s lifetime.

title: Bay City, Michigan Fire Department Owney tag
dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 1 1/4 in. (4.13 x 3.18 cm)
descriptions: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. It was placed on his collar by members of the Bay City, Michigan Fire Department during an 1896 visit. A number of railroad lines traveled through Bay City, including the Grand Rapids & Indiana; Wabash; Chicago & Western Michigan; Michigan Central; and Manistee & Northeastern railroads.
